speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, can the Prime Minister advise the house what results, if any, have followed from conversations held yesterday among members of the government, the premier of Nova Scotia, union and company officials, concerning the cut-backs in the Nova Scotia coal industry?
Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, as the Leader of the Opposition stated yesterday, we had a meeting with the premier of Nova Scotia, the representatives of the Dominion Coal Company and the labour union, the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Mac-Innis), as well as various ministers, the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois), the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Brooks) and the Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell). We discussed in general the situation created in Nova Scotia in consequence of the fact that 1,400,000 tons of coal are piled up and are at the moment unsaleable, although there are orders on hand for the disposal of some 4 million tons in the foreseeable future.
I want to say first that the manner in which the representations were made, both on the part of the company and on the part of the representatives of the unions, was deserving of the highest compliment. There was obviously a desire on the part of both to present a picture, and one of deep concern, not only to those directly affected, namely the miners in Nova Scotia and their families, but also to the economy in general of Nova Scotia and indirectly of the maritimes.
The representations that were made are now receiving the consideration of the government. It is a complex problem; it is one that deserves the fullest consideration. What the decision will be I cannot at the moment say. The cabinet met this morning and discussed the question in all its ramifications, and will also give it further consideration later today.
Having regard to the size of the problem and its great importance, I will say no more than that every sympathetic consideration will be given to assure the bringing about of a state of affairs which will ameliorate to the maximum degree possible this very trying and serious problem. My feelings in that regard and those of my colleagues in the cabinet have certainly been intensified as a result of the co-operative attitude displayed by the representatives of the company and the union. I cannot go further at the present time, except to assure the Leader of the Opposition that this matter is one of preeminent importance.

Inquiries of the Ministry Mr. H. W. Herridge (Kootenay West): I
should like to ask the Prime Minister a supplementary question. Does a situation such as this concern the Borden commission, and have they made any interim reports or recommendations to meet such a situation?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the
moment I can see no connection superficially between the situation in the mines of Nova Scotia and the problems that are faced by the Borden commission. It may be that on closer examination there might be some direct connection, but certainly any decision that will be made will not in any way derogate from the problems faced by the Borden commission or the recommendations the commission will make.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: GATT-STATEMENT AS TO RENEWAL OF AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Springfield asked me several questions which I should like to answer now. The first question was:
When will the general agreement on tariffs and trade ... be up for renewal?
The answer is that GATT continues automatically in effect among the countries wishing to participate, and the question of its termination or renewal therefore does not arise. The next meeting of GATT countries is scheduled for October of this year. As far as the schedules of tariff rates that have been negotiated under GATT are concerned, these are at the present time bound against increase 
for a firm period until January 1, 1961. This, of course, is subject to the renegotiation of particular tariff rates under established GATT procedures.
The second question was:
Will representations be made at that time to the effect that Canada's position be recognized in a special category?
I am not sure what is meant by this question. Should the government at any time consider that special arrangements within GATT should be made with regard to Canada's position, this could, of course, be taken up with our other GATT partners. However, as I stated at the twelfth session of GATT last year in Geneva, the government's position at the present time is that we shall continue to operate our policies in accordance with the rules and procedures of GATT.
The third question referred to the likelihood of the agreement not being renewed by the congress of the United States. I have no comment to make on possible action by another country.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I hasten to make a few observations concerning the recent budget brought down by the Minister of Finance. As one of the members from northern Ontario I assure you that it is still a stronghold of Liberalism, and I am sure it will remain that way for some time to come.
Following this recent election, when not one Conservative was elected in northern Ontario, it is easy to understand why the Conservatives would be concerned with this situation. In a newspaper article which appeared not long after the election I noticed a statement to the effect that the Conservative national organizer was considering taking a trip to northern Ontario to study just why this catastrophe had happened to the Tory party. I do not believe it will do him much good should he take this trip, as I firmly believe that the best informed and most intellectual electors live in the various parts of northern Ontario.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And in Newfoundland.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This, I am sure, shows a firm belief in Liberalism, and I see no reason why any of the electors in the north should ever depart from it.
In the minister's budget there are certain irregularities that I feel I should bring to the government's attention. The Conservative government's budget forecasts a deficit of
[Mr. Hees.l
$648 million. This figure must be viewed with some reserve and suspicion, and certainly should be subjected to further analysis. As recorded at page 1240 of Hansard the Minister of Finance stated in his budget speech: After studying all the available data most carefully and taking account of possible lapsings and our continued search for economies, I have come to the conclusion that our budgetary expenditures for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1959, will he approximately $5,300 million.
Is this figure realistic? Let us begin with the expenditure proposals that are already known and which we find in the tabled main estimates and the first of the supplementary estimates, totalling the sum of $5,237 million. To this must be added payments to the provinces under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act of $70 million, the deficit in the old age security fund of $190 million and the deficit for the Canadian National Railways of $55 million. We then arrive at a total of $5,552 million.
In addition we must add rough estimates for additional statutory requirements and the usual final supplementary estimates totalling $50 million, and payments under the Agricultural Stabilization Act of $3 million, which give a total of $5,605 million. We must also take into consideration unknown expenditure factors including salary increases for civil servants and armed forces personnel, which could amount to $100 million, and further revisions in the dominion-provincial tax rental agreement which could amount to $150 million should Ontario be granted its demand for $78 million.
Assuming that no action is taken by the government with respect to salary increases and upward revision of payments to the provinces, our budgetary expenditures for the year ending March 31, 1959, appear to be approximately $300 million more than the $5,300 million estimates of the minister. Accepting his estimate of revenue of $4,652 million, we find that the budgetary deficit amounts to $5,605 million minus $4,652 million or a total of $953 million.
We now must take into consideration a bookkeeping transfer to budgetary revenue, I suppose, from a non-budgetary national defence equipment account which amounts to $165 million. This bookkeeping shift was evidently taken into consideration by the minister in arriving at his budgetary deficit. If we do the same our estimated $953 million deficit is cut down to $788 million, or $140 million more than the figure that is being quoted so widely. This $788 million deficit presupposes no governmental action on salary increases or increased transfer payments to the provinces. It is difficult to assume that nothing will in fact be done in these two

problem areas. Hence the concern regarding the presently forecast budgetary deficit of only $648 million, and the suspicion that future events will probably bring this deficit figure up to $1 billion.
In times of stress no one argues with the necessity for a deficit budget. However, the full and proper figures should be given and no attempt made to pull the wool over the eyes of the Canadian people when a budget such as this is presented. True figures should be shown, and I believe this has not been done.
It should also be borne in mind that the purpose of this deficit budgeting was to correct unemployment. I will admit that employment figures have increased in the last month, but the over-all number of unemployed is still higher than it should be, and certainly higher than it has been in many years; and now the Canadian taxpayer is faced with both a deficit budget and unemployment. It has not cured the ills it was intended to cure, and this money has to be recovered in one way or another from the taxpayers of Canada at a future date.
Some time ago, Mr. Speaker, I had occasion to say a few words concerning the plight of the small businessman, and I was hoping that some relief for him might have been indicated in this budget. Unfortunately this does not seem to be the case and he is no better off; in fact he is worse off as each day goes by. I am sure it would not have cost the government a great deal of money should the small businessman have been allowed accelerated depreciation on any alterations or renovations he might want to make in his place of business. This would have been of assistance, but it was not contained in the budget.
I feel that the small businessman is being overlooked due to the scarcity of such men in this house; therefore he has not been able to shout loud enough to reach the ears of the mighty. I place myself in the category of a small businessman, and it is for this reason I am attempting to bring the situation to the attention of the government.
At the time I spoke I mentioned that I felt the attention of the combines investigation commission should be drawn to some of the practices which are prevalent and are very harmful at this time. I know that representations have been made to this commission and to various ministers by various retail organizations regarding the use of loss leaders by many of the larger businesses. These loss leaders are used as an attraction to customers to visit their premises where they may pick up other merchandise which shows a respectable profit.
Just recently I received in the mail an advertisement of one of the large business
The Budget-Mr. Mitchell firms in the city of Toronto dealing in furniture, and I should like to mention two articles which I think the house will agree with me are certainly "come-on" merchandise. I hold the advertisement in my hand, and I draw the attention of the house to a very well-known product, namely Kleenex, which in this advertisement reads, "Regular 19 cents a box, on sale two for 19 cents." I assure hon. members that this merchandise cannot be purchased wholesale at nearly this price. Therefore it is in the category of a loss leader.
However, this is not bad enough. This is a business firm which sells furniture, but in the other corner of the advertisement we find this: "Fresh today, Sunbeam bread, 5 cents a loaf". I reiterate, this is a furniture store which has no connection with the sale of bread, but as a come-on is advertising it at 5 cents a loaf. Any hon. member who has been sent out to buy a loaf of bread knows what the approximate regular price should be.
This is a practice which I feel should be stopped. I am sure it is not the intention of any government to allow this to continue, as it, along with many other loss leaders, is detrimental to the small businessman who is trying to make a living and provide a home for his family. I would urge the government to take steps as soon as possible to organize the committee, which they have suggested, to look into this practice which is being followed every day and prevent many small businesses from being forced to the wall and closing up shop.
In the budget, Mr. Speaker, legislation was brought down indicating that prescribed medicines are to be allowed as deductions for income tax purposes. I feel that this legislation is quite in order. As a pharmacist I believe this will be a great relief to persons who have lingering illnesses which cost considerable money, and relief in this way will be welcomed by many families. However, as a pharmacist I must draw attention to the extra work it will entail in each drug store in the recording, filing and giving of receipts for such medication. It will place the pharmacist in a rather embarrassing position if some of his customers should mislay their receipts and at income tax time hurry to him in the hope that he can give them copies. We are pleased to do this, but the amount of work entailed in hunting back over records is going to be tremendous and a tax on the staff who are already overloaded with regulations, the keeping of records and so forth, far in excess of any other type of retail business.
I also wish to draw the minister's attention to the wording he has used in his budget

The Budget-Mr. Thomas speech, which I feel does not fit the circumstances and I hope will be altered when the resolution is brought down. I refer to the wording in the budget speech as follows:
Accounts paid after June 17, 1958, for drugs and medicines which have been prescribed in writing by a medical practioner to be included in the medical expenses in computing taxable income.
The words "in writing" do not seem to be appropriate. Under present regulations of the Department of National Health and Welfare and through pharmacy acts in various provinces we are allowed to take certain types of prescriptions over the telephone and reduce these to writing over the doctor's signature in the form of a prescription, with the pharmacist's signature as well. Therefore I believe this resolution, as far as the wording is concerned, should be changed to read "Legal prescription" or "prescribed medication" instead of the words "in writing". This could be worded in another way which would provide that drugs, medications and so forth which have been prescribed by a medical practitioner, a dentist, a veterinarian surgeon and so on, and recorded by a licensed pharmacist, can be included as expenses that are deductible for income tax purposes. Any of these three wordings would be quite acceptable and should be used in preference to the words "in writing".
I hope the resolution, therefore, will be appropriately reworded, and that supervision will be given by the department's inspectors so that only drugs and pharmaceutical preparations are allowed as prescribed items. If this is not done many other articles could be included in the form of a prescribed order, which is not intended in the legislation and would add considerably to the amount of money this legislation would cost the government. I assure the house that we pharmacists are quite willing to assist in this relief for our customers, but certain pitfalls could be encountered which I hope will be thoroughly investigated to prevent any unfair advantage being taken of this legislation. Representations have already been made by our Canadian pharmaceutical association to the deputy minister of finance, and I believe certain questions have been ironed to everyone's satisfaction, with a view to having this legislation run smoothly and achieve the purpose for which it is intended.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. H. A. Thomas (Middlesex West):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased indeed to have a part in this debate. I have listened with interest to the speeches which have been made by opposition members as well as by members of our own party. I should like to

contribute to the congratulations which have already been offered from all parts of the house to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) on this excellent budget.
This is a moderate budget, well balanced, designed to maintain a balance between the forces of depression and the forces of inflation. I think even the members of the opposition will agree that the Minister of Finance has done an acceptable job in this regard. I have noted some of the comments from members of the opposition. The Liberal financial critic, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson), made these statements at page 1279 of Hansard for June 17:
The budget contains very little for the Canadian people except cheaper rat poison, violins, cut flowers and tree guards not more than 36 inches in height.
Again, at page 1279 the hon. member said:
We have a deficit not by design but a deficit by default.
My analysis of what is lacking in this budget is that the government is simply sitting out the situation and sitting it out on its hands.
Then he takes a slightly different line on page 1463, after he has had several days to think it over. On June 20, he said:
One can certainly argue for spending and deficits if they are not aimless but rather are planned, comprehensive and vigorous enough proposals to provide incentive, to provide lift, to perk up the economy. But I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that an analysis of this budget will show that the deficit is more attributable to political commitments than to economic theory or for the relief of unemployment.
Farther along on the opposition side we have the leader of the C.C.F. group, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), who had this to say on June 20 as found at page 1470 of Hansard:
This is an ice water budget which I think will awaken the people of Canada to the fact that on March 31 they were cheated, as has been proven by the government's lack of action since that date.
Again, on page 1471 the same speaker went on to say:
This government, with its double talk, with its progressive face of last year and its Tory face of this year is just as inconsistent in all its actions.
On page 1472 he went on to say:
-Conservatives all over this country, whether they be high-placed Conservatives in Ontario or high-placed Conservatives with another name in the province of Quebec, have all got their elbows or their arms into this very lucrative deal, or as somebody says, their nose in the trough. They are still exempt. There is no capital gains tax.
As found on the same page the hon. member went on to say:
The agricultural producers of this country expected fair treatment by this government. They put great stock in the Agricultural Stabilization Act passed in this house last year, . . . The legislation says the farmer is to have the cost

of production, but the government are not trying to find out what the cost of production is.
I think those are good and typical examples of the line of criticism put forward by both parties on the opposition side. We are dealing now with the Liberal amendment to the motion to go into committee of ways and means. That amendment is in these words:
That all the words after the word "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
' This house regrets that the government, in its budget proposals, has failed to cope satisfactorily with the problems of the recession in spite of the largest peacetime deficit in Canadian history and that it is moving towards greater trade restrictions at a time when other countries in the western world are moving in the opposite direction."
I think possibly we should congratulate the official opposition for the efforts they have put forth in criticism of the budget. I think we can congratulate them for the reason that they had so little to work with that their efforts indicate great industry in their search for arguments with which to do their job. The budget has little in it to criticize, and in view of that fact the efforts of the opposition are to be commended.
With respect to the criticism that the government is following an aimless course and that its actions are unplanned, surely the opposition will remember those items which have been enumerated again and again, and which disprove that criticism. The actions of the government have been well planned, and ever since the government took office a little over a year ago they have been aimed at accomplishing certain purposes. The country was slipping into a depressed economic state. The aim of the new Conservative government was to stop that trend, to bring about a measure of greater prosperity, and to create a more buoyant economy.
The actions they took are well known. They began immediately by making more money available for housing, and during the last year over half a billion dollars has been made available for that purpose. Social security allowances of all kinds, old age security, old age assistance and disability allowances, were all increased with the object of placing more purchasing power in the hands of the people so that our markets and business generally could be stimulated and our manufacturing industries could get back to work and relieve unemployment, which was increasing to proportions very undesirable in this country.
Income taxes were eased; a total of $178 million a year was lopped off such taxes. The results of these actions have been to reduce interest rates so that money is more readily available. The recession has been slowed
The Budget-Mr. Thomas down, and there is reason to believe that the bottom has been reached and we are again on the upgrade.
For the same purpose, to create a more buoyant economy and also to assist agriculture, which was bearing a greater share of the burden of recession than other parts of the economy, the Agricultural Stabilization Act was passed. The government has taken action under this legislation to improve the position of agriculture and again to get more money into the hands of the people with which to buy manufactured commodities.
The government is also encouraging all segments of our economy to hold the price line in an effort to prevent further spirals of inflation. I would think these actions are neither aimless nor unplanned. They have produced results and will continue to produce results. Therefore the criticism of the opposition cannot be taken too seriously.
Now I should say a word about our Middlesex West constituency. Our riding is located just west of the city of London in southwestern Ontario. Due to the moderate climate and the nature of the soil we have probably as great a diversity of industry in this riding as will be found in any riding in Canada. We have good soil of all types, with the result that crops which will flourish and grow anywhere in Canada can be grown in Middlesex West, and they are grown there in great abundance-cannery crops, tobacco, fruits of all kinds, potatoes, grain, hay-and we have also large areas of some of the finest grazing land to be found anywhere in the world.
Our livestock production is varied and important. We have a large dairying industry, and some of the finest herds of dairy cattle that are to be found anywhere in Canada are located in our area of Middlesex West. Some sheep are raised there, but not in large numbers. Also there is an important production of hogs. Our poultry production is important. We have some of the largest turkey farms to be found anywhere in the land. Another item of major importance is the production of seed. We grow a great deal of registered grain for seed. Again, being close to large centres of population, we have a large and important greenhouse industry for the production of vegetables and flowers.
Based on this agricultural production we have a number of processing industries. We have one of the largest canning factories in the country located in the town of Strathroy, one of a chain of factories which once belonged to Canadian Canners and which still operates under that name, although control has passed to a United States interest. Another very

The Budget-Mr. Thomas important industry in that area is the teed mixing industry. Every town and village has one plant or more which grinds grain and mixes it with supplements for stock feed. As western towns have their strings of elevators along the railway tracks, the towns and villages of Middlesex West have these feed mills which distribute feed mixes to the farmers.
We have a large flour mill in the town of Strathroy. We also have a very large cold storage warehouse where fruit and potatoes are stored and later packed for the trade. We have, in the riding of Middlesex West, what is reputed to be the largest egg breaking plant in the British empire, where eggs are broken and frozen and shipped all over the world. We used to dry them there and make egg powder during the war. I do not know whether that process is still being carried on; I think not. These eggs are transported in a frozen state. We have quite a number of egg and poultry processing plants where fowls are dressed and prepared for sale to the distributing trade. We also have a very large milk gathering station in Middlesex West. Milk is transported 25 to 30 miles to the station. It is cooled there and taken in large trucks to the processing plant at Aylmer. Also we have in our riding a very large seed-cleaning establishment, where carloads of seed of all kinds are prepared not only for local sale but for shipment to the United States.
Not only do we have these processing plants connected with agriculture, but in the towns in our riding we have a number of medium-sized plants which manufacture products not connected with agriculture. We have a large aluminum plant which manufactures window sashes and other building fixtures; we have a plant for the manufacture of mobile homes, otherwise called trailers, and we have a large furniture factory. We have a number of lumber mills which saw hardwood lumber for export to all parts of the country.
Our area produces fine oak timber in addition to cherry, walnut, maple, elm and all other kinds of hardwood. It is rather strange, when you ride through the towns in this area, to see on one side of the track large piles of lumber which have been sawn ready for shipment to furniture plants in other parts of the country, and on the other side of the track large piles of lumber which have been unloaded from British Columbia or northwest Alberta for use in the building trade in our own area. Hardwood is of no use for outside purposes; its use is for furniture and inside fittings. Therefore, though we produce large quantities of hardwood, it cannot be used locally except in our local furniture industry.


We have woollen mills for the making of blankets, knitting mills for socks, and we have one of the largest nursery enterprises in the country, the head office of which is in Middlesex West in the town of Strathroy with branches in Bowmanville and Abbotsford, Quebec. Then we have a large handle factory operated by the Welland Vale Manufacturing Company. There is also a large distribution plant for heating equipment-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was just about to relate these things to the budget debate.
I was pointing out the variety in agriculture and manufacturing industries, and raising the point that the budget introduced by our government aims to improve our position and to assist these industries which are being carried on in Middlesex West. What is required there in general is a certain amount of protection for our industries. The budget in its supplementary papers has mentioned certain tariff changes which are designed to assist industries through our part of Ontario. Because the protection is needed the minister and the government are to be commended because of these protective measures. Because of our position in a northern latitude it is possible to grow agricultural products farther south more cheaply than we can produce them, and to get them on the market earlier than ours can be placed on the market. A certain amount of protection is therefore required for our agricultural products. Because our industries are not large in nature, a certain amount of protection is required to keep them going.
The budget deals with the stabilization of agricultural products. It expressed the hope that large payments under the agricultural prices stabilization act will not be required. I have already complimented the government on their efforts to stabilize agriculture through the action taken under this agricultural prices stabilization act. I have read some criticism that has been offered by members of the opposition to the effect that this stabilization act is not altogether serving the purpose for which it was intended. I contend that the stabilization act has done a good job. Agricultural prices can never be set so that everyone will be satisfied. In trying

to arrive at satisfactory levels for prices I think the government has made a worthwhile effort to satisfy the farmer as well as to protect the interests of all concerned.
A large number of products are now stabilized or supported, and these support prices range from 80 per cent to 112 per cent of the base price. People in Middlesex West are generally satisfied, I understand, with the action that has been taken with regard to eggs, and for the most part with regard to dairy products. There has been some disappointment over the level of the price for soybeans, but the differences of opinion which have arisen concerning the prices of soybeans, I submit, are mostly due to the lack of any acceptable figures covering the cost of production and the lack of cost of production figures generally in the industry of agriculture.
The best figures available-and they were produced under the auspices of the economics branch of the Ontario department of agriculture-indicate that soybeans can be produced for about $1.41 per bushel, that corn can be produced for about 88 cents per bushel, and that the cost of producing sugar beets is about $9.90 per ton. There might be some agreement among the farmers as to the cost of producing a ton of sugar beets; a great deal of research has been done in that regard. However, I do not think anyone has succeeded yet in persuading the farmer that soybeans can be produced for $1.41 per bushel. However, those are the best figures available, and until the farmers or our agricultural research experts can bring forward proof that these figures are not sound, we must accept them.
With soybeans supported at $2.10 per bushel, on the basis of these figures, which are the best available, there cannot be too much complaint. The soybean producers themselves feel that they should have $3 per bushel in order to put them in a sound position in the production of soybeans. They asked for a support price of $2.57 per bushel. The government, after taking all things into consideration, set the support price at $2.10 per bushel. I know our soybean growers are not happy about this situation. Personally I am not happy but we must commend the government for using their best judgment and doing the best they could under the circumstances.
I should like to say a word about the Canada Water Conservation Act of 1953. In the riding of Middlesex West we have two conservation authorities. The one of particular interest to us is the Ausable valley
The Budget-Mr. Thomas authority, which takes in most of the northern part of the constituency. There is another authority in Middlesex county, namely the upper Thames valley conservation authority, which is of more interest to Middlesex East than it is to Middlesex West. I cannot see anything in the budget which will give any measure of assistance to those authorities over and above the provisions of the water conservation assistance legislation. These river valley conservation authorities include all the municipalities which have land draining into any of the tributaries of the entire river system, and each municipality appoints representatives to serve on those authorities. The conservation authorities are something like a municipal government or school board, having wide and important powers and responsibilities; and once set up they have full control over conservation in the various watersheds.
I would like to make the proposal that the federal government, when considering assistance to these conservation authorities, should include the whole conservation scheme planned by such authorities rather than limit consideration to individual items in an over-all plan. That is to say, rather than taking the attitude that one particular dam, for instance, was not of sufficient importance to justify federal assistance, several dams and other works should be all taken together when such consideration is being given to water conservation schemes.
The present water conservation legislation was criticized in the June 23, 1958 report of the standing committee on mines, forests and waters. The minister himself pointed out that this act is not giving the service which he feels it might give in providing assistance to these conservation authorities, and he made the suggestion that the legislation be reviewed with the object of making it more useful.
Time does not permit me to go into much further detail, but I would like to mention that in Middlesex West we have an Indian reserve, and that I feel it is desirable to help the Indians on that reservation to develop their agricultural resources more intensively than has been done in past years. A great deal of agricultural activity was carried on at that particular reservation prior to the first world war, but owing to its proximity to several large industrial centres the Indians since that time have tended to accept positions in industry rather than engage in agriculture. Some of the older Indians have now, however, reached the conclusion that they would be better advised to develop more agriculture on their reservation and a committee has been set up

The Budget-Mr. Bourque among them to promote this idea. We have been promised the co-operation of the Indian affairs branch in connection with this project. The Indian affairs officials feel, however, that the promotion of greater agricultural activity on the reserve should come from the Indians themselves rather than from the officers of the Indian affairs branch.
In conclusion, I would again like to commend the minister and the government upon the budget, and to urge its adoption without amendment.

Now, Mr. Speaker, for the fiscal year 1957-58, the Minister of Finance of the day had forecast a surplus of $152 million. The present Minister of Finance, who claimed he could offer surpluses too, and achieve all sorts of good things, has unfortunately offered the people of Canada nothing but a $39 million deficit.
During the fiscal year 1956-1957, the Liberals reduced the federal debt by $522 million through a budgetary surplus of $258 million, a non-budgetary surplus of $166 million and a reduction on cash account of $98 million, totalling $522 million.
But that is not all Mr. Speaker. The Liberals reduced the debt by $2,500 million since the end of the war. For this year the
1702	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Bourque Minister of Finance forecasts a deficit of $648 million and, at the same time, he says that he will require close to $3,400 million. He estimates his revenue at $4,660 million. Expenditures, that is to say the main and supplementary estimates, will amount to $5,237 million. If to this figure we add $70 million for the hospital insurance plan, another $55 million for the expected C.N.R. deficit, $190 million for a deficit in the old age security fund, another $100 million for civil service salary increases because a raise of 8 per cent was definitely promised, and the other supplementary estimates which will certainly amount to no less than $100 million, we reach a total of $5,752 million.
Considering an estimated revenue of $4,660 million, the actual budget deficit is $1,092 million.
That is not all, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of Finance has further claimed that public debt will increase by $1,400 million, that is $775 million against the exchange fund, plus a $648 million deficit, which gives a total of $1,423 million. I claim however that the debt will increase by $1,092 million, to which must be added $775 million from the exchange fund, which gives a total of $1,867 million.
If you consider that Mr. Frost, the premier of Ontario, has asked for $100 million, an amount of $300 million must be added to that figure-taking the equalization principle into account-which will give for this year an actual increase of $2,167 million in our debt.
From 1947 to 1957, the Liberals have reduced the debt by some $2,500 million. Well, Mr. Speaker, in spite of all the promises made by the Conservatives, in spite of all they said during the election campaign, if my figures are correct, and I have every reason to believe they are, the Minister of Finance will have increased our debt by $2,167 million in a single year.
Mr. Speaker, I read in the Petit Journal of last Sunday an article entitled: "Thank you just the same, Mr. Fleming!" in which the author said:
How shall we spend those 49 cents?
Sixteen million Canadians will save S8 million in taxes between now and the end of the year. That is about 50 cents each.
Mr. Speaker, that saving represents less than one cent a week. What a farce! Especially after we had been promised prosperity and many great things. And what are Canadians getting now? Unemployment. In fact, this very week automobile workers gathered at


the door of the parliament buildings, carrying signs which read: "We do not want charity, we want work".
If we had a deficit of two or even three billion dollars but provided jobs, with prospects of returning prosperity in a not too distant future, it would not be too bad. We would just say: "We went through a depression, and we are back on our feet". But what is the Conservative party offering us today? Nothing! Just misery! That is what we will have to face next winter.
Mr. Speaker, I contend that if the Liberals were able to reduce the national debt by $2,500 million in a ten year period, it is outrageous that the Conservatives should have increased it by $2,167 million in a single year.

One thing that worries me very much today is the anti-Americanism we find creeping across Canada. I think the government, if given the necessary time-and I am sure we will be here for a long time-will iron out all the inconsistencies that arose between the former Liberal government and the government of the United States. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at one o'clock when the house rose for lunch I was discussing the inadequate policy of the Liberal party with regard to the trade and economic report which was tabled in the house last January. In this report the Liberal party were told certain things and 1 believe they did not act upon them. Their tight money policy was not the proper thing. I believe their immigration policy was poor and, most of all, they could have put money into housing in the early part of last year but they did not do so.
It is most gratifying to see that the unemployment situation in Canada is not quite as serious as it was, with 150,000 fewer people on the unemployment rolls and 212,000 more people at work.
With regard to the trade policies of the late government, the imbalance of trade between Canada and the United States grew to astronomical proportions after 1950 until in the early part of 1957 it was $1,300 million. I believe the Conservative party is on the right track with regard to commonwealth relations. We are not ignoring the United States. We want the United States to know the facts with regard to the economic conditions of this country, and we want to secure an understanding of our problems. With the commonwealth conference in the fall I am sure we can expand our trade throughout the commonwealth and the world.
Talking about deficit spending, we have heard pro and con on this question, but it seems funny to me to hear criticism of deficit spending, when during the election campaign the Leader of the Opposition talked about tax holidays, $400 million tax cuts and so on, thus increasing our present deficit. I am not too clear on the thinking of the Liberal party with regard to this, but most of all I am not too clear on the thinking of the C.C.F. party. They would have us spend billions of dollars. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), who is not in his seat at the present time, talked to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) about contradictions.

If the house will bear with me for one moment I should like to talk about the C.C.F. party and their policy with regard to financing. During the election campaign, the C.C.F. spokesman in my riding stated that if they came to power they would raise taxes. In a public debate I asked my opponent if this were so, and he said: Oh, yes, we would raise the taxes from the big corporations and the millionaires. I proceeded to ask: Is it not also the policy of the C.C.F. party to nationalize the steel mills that is: the Steel Co. of Canada, Dofasco, the Firestone Company and several other companies prominent in Hamilton? He said: That is the policy; we are going to take everything for the workingman. I fail to see how the C.C.F. party could raise the taxes of the big corporations and take them over at the same time. I think it is very inconsistent.
I went further, and asked my opponent how they were going to take over these big corporations, and he said they were going to purchase their stock. I think the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) in his alphabetical speech talked about robbing the people. In taking over this stock I think the C.C.F. would be robbing all the people of Canada, not only the millionaires but the little people who hold stock in these corporations. I asked, referring to a certain type of stock, whether they would pay $30 the market value. They said: No, we would pay the market value when the stock first came into force. So I believe their policies of nationalization and increasing taxation are very unsound and ridiculous.
In this budget I believe the Minister of Finance has done the best job possible considering what he had to put up with and what was left by the Liberal party after 22 years in power. They had the facts, and they did not act upon them. How different was the amendment which the hon. Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), proposed during the last 1957 budget debate when the Hon. Walter Harris was minister of finance. He moved:
That this house regrets that the economic policy of the government fails, despite a very large surplus, to meet the needs of the Canadian people and in particular (a) does not provide adequately for old age and other pensioners; (b) does not propose a reduction in the personal income tax; (c) does not assure to the provinces a larger share of the revenues from federal-provincial fields of taxation; and (d) ignores the problems and needs of agriculture.
Mr. Speaker, this was true Conservative policy. We were putting forth views at that time which we thought were right. In the last session of Conservative administration every one of those amendments was put into 57071-3-108
The Budget-Mr. Peters effect by the Conservative party, and the people of Canada are getting benefits from them today.
In summarizing my short speech I should like to say that the Conservative party is a very progressive party. Some of the Liberals feel we are conservatives with a small "c". On the other hand they think we are the old Tories of the depression years. But we are a party of young men and we are going to try to show Canada that we have good policies; that we have bound the French and the English together without disunity, without taking the east coast from Upper Canada or Quebec from Ontario, and with this kind of thinking I believe we will have one Canada for Canadians.

speechtext:
In rising to speak on this budget I find many things in it about which I am not too happy, and very little to give the Canadian people encouragement in the years to come.
One of the things that struck me particularly was the great play that has been made on what the situation is going to be in the coming year. We were told in the budget that our gross national product was going to rise by approximately two per cent. That, I would say, appears to be a very liberal estimate of what the situation is likely to be. At the same time, very little was made of the fact that our national population is continuing to grow by a similar amount each year by natural increase. So it would look as if our situation is going to be worse this year in the light of the gross national product in terms of the population we are going to have, and therefore the situation does not look too bright or too hopeful for the forthcoming year.
I, personally, am not in agreement with having a deficit budget unless that deficit budget is going to satisfy some particular purpose, and it would appear to me that the budget we have before us is no different from the last budget that the Liberal government introduced in March, 1957. There have been very few changes, but I think those few changes are things that the Canadian people should look at very closely. It reminds me of the fact that governments, irrespective of their political colour, are faced with certain housekeeping expenses, and with regard to these the Conservatives are going to find it very difficult to depart from the policy followed by the Liberals in the past. And, I may say, the C.C.F. party also would have to make this type of payment, and that this part of the budget-this housekeeping budget-would be the same no matter what the government was. The small percentage with regard to which the government can make a difference

The Budget-Mr. Peters because of its political views seems to be getting less and less. Certainly this budget would seem to indicate that.
I think an emphasis has been put on certain phases in that budget which would indicate some minor trends of a difference in thinking between the Conservatives and the Liberals. We notice this in the tariff proposals. I think it is surprising that a party which comes to power and which brings in its first budget after so many years should not have done some thinking about the protectionist views it held 20, 30 or 40 years ago and come up with something a little better than a patched up tariff program of this sort. The tariff structure should have been examined in the light of the new thinking that is taking place throughout the world and certainly in the light of the offer of free trade extended by the United Kingdom government, and it should have taken into consideration the fact that in Europe free trade on a united basis is the policy of many of those countries.
I think that this budget failed to take into consideration what must be the experience of many years and has reverted, in relation to this tariff structure, back to the thinking of the Conservatives many years ago. There are many things that we wished to have done, and I am quite happy that the hon. member for Hamilton South (Mr. McDonald), should have mentioned some of them. Some of the things which I think it necessary to raise and to give consideration to for the welfare of the bulk of our population were not mentioned. I refer, for instance, to family allowances. In 1945 the Conservatives were quite opposed to family allowances. But this is something to which we have become accustomed. It is something that I am quite sure the Conservative government would not wish to take away from the Canadian people. If they do not wish to take it away from the Canadian people, then they also have an obligation to bring it back to its original purchasing power, a procedure which would give us now family allowances of approximately twice what we are receiving. This would not be any increase, I might suggest, but it would be rather in keeping with the cost of living.
I think that raises another problem that we should face up to. We are now enjoying the highest costs-and most of us are not liking it-that we have ever had in the consumer field. Everything we buy is double, triple and sometimes much higher than that. At the same time we in Canada are faced with a recession. Although the government may not feel that this recession is important or should be given any particular consideration in this first budget of this parliament,

I think it certainly deserves some consideration, and that a great deal must be done to eliminate that problem. It is true that those who are employed are finding that their wages are up as compared to what they were ten years ago but they are also finding at the same time that those wages do not buy in produce as much as they bought ten years ago. Hence we must face this inflationary problem if we are going to look after the people in Canada. In order to do that I suggest that raising family allowances is a way of getting into the people's pockets money that they would not otherwise normally have.
This also is true with respect to old age security. It is quite true-and I do not think there is a member of this house who will disagree-that the main reason the Conservative government was elected in June, 1957 was the fact that they offered the old age pensioners of this country an increase in the old age pension. But I do not think that they were even honest with themselves when they raised that pension by $9. They had promised more than this and they had not made it pie in the sky. I note that the hon. member shakes his head. It is quite true that they may not have been definite because they seldom if ever are definite about anything; but you must tie it to something. You cannot go to the voters and say, "We will give you an increase" without being able to justify it in some way. The only logical justification for the increase, when our revenues are not as high as we should like to see them, is on the basis of maintaining purchasing power which we wish to maintain. I think this matter must be given some consideration in the near future.
We were pleased that an investigation should be set up to examine the whole structure of old age security. I think we all realize that while we can make promises at election time, we are finally going to have to implement them; and that procedure costs money. I am told that we are now going in the red quite rapidly on our old age security program. But why the investigation in the United States? I do not credit Canadian governments over the years with having been so unaware of the situation and so unaware of the lack of a formula on which to base their old age pension system that they did not look at other pension schemes throughout the world, not only that in the United States but those in other countries. I am quite sure that the officials in the minister's department could tell the minister exactly what the program is in the United States and how it could be applied in Canada, and that we did not need to stall for a year or so while we made a phony investigation into something we already knew.

The C.C.F. believes in and would implement the $75 old age pension. We also agree that it cannot be raised in the manner in which we have raised pensions in the past. We propose to the Canadian people to provide two types of old age security, one that is a basic old age security similar to the one that we enjoy but at a reasonable rate in line with the cost of living; and second, we propose that there be a contributary old age pension or national pension or superannuation plan or whatever you might wish to call it, and that this plan be of a nature that the employee be compelled to contribute out of his wages, that the employer also be compelled to pay a like amount out of his fund and that the federal government maintain and operate this plan in a manner similar to that in which the unemployment insurance system that we enjoy today is handled. That would mean that when an employee quits one job he could go to another job and carry his pension fund with him, that he would establish this pension plan from the day he began to work, that he would have an equity in the plan and that he would be able to carry it from job to job, industry to industry or province to province and that at the end of his lifetime of work he would be able to retire on a plan to which he had helped to contribute.
The first step I would suggest in this proposed plan would be to eliminate this $60 limit that we have put on people that are well able to afford a higher payment. We say that all people, even those who have not been employed like your wife and mine-we do not consider them to have actually been employed-should be able to enjoy the basic pension of $75, and we hope they will be able to do so; and we think that one of the steps that must be taken into consideration and should have been taken into consideration in this budget is that of allowing the tax to rise as the income of the people rises. If there is any truth in the statement that the wealth of this country is rising and that the people themselves are sharing in it, then even the $60 a month that was put on a number of years ago would not be realistic if we used the same formula from which the original amount of money was raised.
We have heard what was said by the hon. member for Hamilton South, and I am quite pleased that he raised this matter. He stated that the C.C.F. had said that they would increase taxation. That is quite true. We would increase certain forms of taxation. What he said with regard to corporation stock or corporations is not true. The C.C.F. at no time have had any desire to nationalize industries just for the sake of nationalization.

If it has not been stated in this particular case, it has been stated in other places in a manner similar to that employed by the hon. member who preceded me. I should like to use one example. In recent months we have seen a particular case in which the federal government is involved namely the matter of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines.
We have seen very large profits made and we do not want to say whether or not those are right although legally we have allowed them to make these huge profits on very low investments. Some companies make an investment of a few hundred dollars and realize a capital gain of $1 million. Certainly we should tax that capital gain. Can any hon. member name any country in the world that does not have a capital gains tax? If the same companies who are spending money in Canada were to spend it in investing in pipe lines in the United States they would have to pay a capital gains tax of 25 per cent. There is no point in giving these people unrestricted profits without requiring something in return. We should remember that they are exploiting the natural resources of Canada. Is there any better way of imposing a tax that will provide the people of Canada with some protection through the means of old age security and other social welfare measures? This could be done by imposing a capital gains tax on those companies that risk very little and make a great profit through exploiting our natural resources.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I
wish now to approach the subject of pipe lines in a different way. As hon. members appreciate, the government made money available for part of the pipe line in the budget. We have received many complaints over the months concerning the Northern Ontario portion of the pipe line. I hold in my hand a letter which I received just the other day which points out better than I could some of the problems the people in that area are facing, and I should like to read a brief excerpt from the letter. Its author states:
Furthermore, the company-
That is, a contractor of the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation-
-has developed a sort of disdain and hatred against our men because they are French-speaking. "The least of them, the better!" is the motto of the said company; this is why our men keep on going every morning to the office and there is no work for them, but the company hires strangers, even from Texas, ignoring the local starving families.
I might point out that the lumber and pulp and paper industry in this area west of Hearst has almost disappeared. Where there were 7,000 or 8,000 workers in the bush last year there are now less than 2,000. These people wish to work on the pipe line in order to support themselves and their families although it is not necessarily the type of work for which they have been trained. Nevertheless they are willing to accept labourers' rates of $1.25 an hour, but they are being refused the opportunity of working on the line. The letter goes on to describe some of the other events that are taking place:
-since the TCP-
The Trans-Canada Pipeline Company-
-compels the men to work Sundays, in spite of all civil and divine laws, claiming that it must make up for time lost during January and February.
While one can appreciate the company's desire to compensate for lost time, I frankly do not think it is a justifiable excuse for having the employees work overtime. I cannot believe that the line will continue to be constructed in northern Ontario during the winter months because there can be anywhere from four to six feet of frost in the ground. There can be no justification for compelling the employees to work on Sunday

when it is not a continuous operation. If it were an around the clock operation there would perhaps be some slight justification for this and the employees could be given their day of rest on another day during the week. There is no reason for having the employees work between 70 and 80 hours a week. Two people could work a 40-hour week on the job and it would be accomplished just as quickly.
With respect to the pipe line, the government has failed to take any action in line with the statements it made prior to the election, on which it was returned to this house. Previous to the election members of that party spoke about nationalization of pipe lines. Not only hon. members of the C.C.F. but the leader of the Conservative party agreed that nationalization would probably be a good thing. I believe the government should seriously take into consideration nationalizing our pipe lines.
I noticed an article in the Globe and Mail of yesterday which reported that the question of nationalization of the trans-Canada pipe line was discussed at a convention of municipalities meeting in Toronto. They agreed that the federal government should be approached and asked to take some action in the nationalization of the pipe line and only two dissenting votes were cast. There are many abuses prevalent on the pipe line which I do not think the Canadian people can afford to tolerate.
At this point I wish to thank the minister for the assistance he provided to the gold miners in my area and on behalf of all gold mining communities in Canada I tender him my appreciation. Having sat in during the presentation of several briefs by the gold mining industry to the federal government I can safely state that those in the industry will appreciate this increased assistance. However, they know and I am sure the minister knows that assistance of this kind is not the solution to the problem. Emergency gold mining assistance is being paid to only a small part of the industry and other parts of the industry struggle along without any aid because their costs of production are not as high as some of the other more marginal mines. The government has not offered a permanent solution to the problem confronting the industry and therefore it has an obligation to the industry. I would suggest that the government remove the word "emergency" from the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act when it is next brought into the house for renewal or revision. There is no longer a need for the word "emergency"

to be there because this appears to be a continuous problem which requires a permanent solution.
I believe the government should investigate the matter of storing gold, which could very well be referred to the banking and commerce committee. Let us put a Fort Knox in Canada. Let us buy the gold and back the currency of our own money. If the United States can afford it at $35 it should be worth $35 and more to us. We could set our price for gold. Other countries have had to do that. I am sure we will find some satisfactory method of utilizing gold other than selling it to the United States, which pays only $35 for our gold. If we feel that the gold mining industry should be saved let us find a permanent solution to the problems it faces instead of dealing with the industry on a day to day, year to year basis.
I want to advise the minister that we in the mining communities of Canada are going to be watching very carefully to make sure that a fair proportion of the 25 per cent or $2J million is returned to the pockets of the workers and through them to the communities that are entirely dependent on that industry. I do not believe the Canadian people have any interest whatever in financing the dividends that are being paid to shareholders in these corporations.
If some of the members on the Conservative benches feel that statement is unfair because they are thinking of some of the dividends from some of these corporations about which they have been speaking, they should take a look at some of these mining companies who are paying out sums as large as $16 million in voluntary dividends when there was an original capital investment of only a quarter of a million dollars. I do not think we have to waste too much sympathy on the gold mines or their operators but we should have a great deal of sympathy and we must be very concerned about those miners who are working for very low wages and who are completely dependent on that industry for their very existence. This is a serious situation throughout northern Ontario and many other parts of Canada. This part of the country must be developed and I therefore hope that every consideration will be given to the people who live in those communities I have mentioned and who, as I say, depend on the mines for their livelihood.
There are a number of other problems in northern Ontario which have not been met by this budget, in fact I can think of very few which have been met by it. However, I am hopeful that some of them will eventually be taken care of. One such problem
The Budget-Mr. Peters is with respect to agriculture. Every day people leave the farms of this nation and I particularly have in mind northern Ontario where you can drive through the country and see signs on the corner posts along the side roads "auction sale, such and such a date" and then there is a list of the farm equipment for sale at the various farms. Agriculture is one of our greatest assets in Canada. The agricultural industry is both staple and basic, an economy which we can improve and expand with very little effort and which can be made more equitable with the economies in other parts of our country and, indeed, with the agricultural economy of other countries. I say this because, as is well known, there are hungry people throughout the world and there is a common need for food. We have the means and the ability to bring about great production in that field. I think some consideration should be given to increasing our ability to sell our products and to increasing the value of those products.
This appears to be the day to talk about Conservative candidates during election time and so I will make reference to the Conservative candidate in my own area who made speeches before and since the last election asking for assistance in respect of beef production in my area. He is quite right. Beef cattle can be raised in northern Ontario better than it can be raised in any other part of Canada. Our climate is very similar to that of western Ontario and with our clay land our produce can equal if not improve upon the produce of any other sections of the country. Mention was made recently by one hon. member of the grain in his area which he said was the top quality. We in northern Ontario have done better than he has to the extent of 30 bushels per day. We need assistance, however, and we would recommend the setting up of government gradings, particularly with respect to cattle so that we may stamp our beef No. 1 quality. Assistance should be given to our farmers in connection with improved breeding of our livestock generally so that our beef production may be increased and made more readily available to Canadian markets.
One suggestion I would like to make is that the government could render assistance in this respect by making provision for a slaughter house in my area and I understand that there are in existence certain acts which would make such assistance possible. We would then be able to eliminate some of this dependence upon gold mines and would be able to branch out into secondary industries. This would serve a double purpose in that the federal government would be relieved of some of its responsibilities in

The Budget-Mr. Peters respect of subsidies now being paid to the mines. These subsidies have constituted a very difficult problem and it has been very difficult to dispose of them.
We will be watching the situation with respect to how this budget is going to be applied for the assistance of those people who came to Ottawa the other day stating that all they asked for was the right to work. It is true that all these people want is a job. It cannot be said that they are lazy or do not want to work. They live in towns such as Windsor where jobs have not been available for a long time, where unemployment benefits have for many months been exhausted and where seasonal benefits no longer apply. We will watch this situation very closely.
This brings us to another matter. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) stood up in the house the other day and very graciously suggested that parliament should sit at 4.30 on July 1 instead of at 2.30. I have been concerned with labour problems for quite a few years and July 1 is one of those holidays which we have had very little difficulty in getting employers to endorse as a national holiday. It is true that with respect to some of the other holidays management has argued that they are not of a national character but this national holiday has been the only one universally observed. This day commemorates the creation of the Dominion of Canada and yet we are asking the representatives of the people of Canada to sit in this house on that day rather than enjoy the holiday celebrations.
