Mr. Speaker, in speaking here for the first time as member for Rimouski, I should like to recall the memory of some of the most prominent figures of Canadian political history who have attached their names to my constituency.
After the principle of responsible government had been accepted, Robert Baldwin became attorney general of Upper Canada and, in accordance with the practices of the time, had to be re-elected but, unfortunately, went down to defeat in his Ontario riding of Hastings. Lafontaine, then member for York, asked the member for Rimouski, one Borne, to resign and, in early 1843, Baldwin was elected by acclamation as member for Rimouski and remained so until the general election of 1844. A few years later, in 1847, Joseph-Charles Tache, was elected member for Rimouski. He represented that riding until 1857.
Mr. Speaker, may I remind hon. members that Joseph-Charles Tache was the founder of the Courrier du Canada and was at one time deputy minister of agriculture, in Ottawa. By articles in his paper and by means of a pamphlet entitled Provinces de VUnion Federate (Provinces of the Federal Union) published in 1858, Tache was one of the main promoters and propagandists of the confederation idea.
Finally, in 1878, Sir Hector Langevin, one of the fathers of confederation-who, after the death of Sir Georges Etienne Cartier, was the principal collaborator of Sir John A. Macdonald, and who was also the brother of the first bishop of Rimouski-tried to get elected in my riding, but unfortunately failed.
Such illustrious precedents, Mr. Speaker, may well fill a young member of parliament with noble ideals, but also with a great deal of humility. I want to say, without boasting, that I have no other ambition than to modestly follow in the steps of these great men.

I congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for presenting us with a very lucid and detailed study of the problem of Canadian finance and of the general economic situation of our country. I congratulate him specially, as I do the government, for developing and deciding to apply an economic and financial policy which, in the present situation, appears to me to be very appropriate.
I congratulate the official financial critic of the opposition,, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson). For all the incoherence of his theories and the built in contradictions of his system, which were very forcibly denounced by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell), I was deeply interested in his speech.
I was surprised to find that our Liberal colleagues base all their disparagement of the budget on the fact that this year the government will have a deficit of about $650 million, when the very A B C of economics say that, in periods of recession, government expenditures should be maintained at a very high level. And while lashing into the announced deficit, Liberal members found it possible to lecture the government for its failure to cut down taxes even more. They inveigled against the budget deficit but asked the government to introduce all sorts of measures that would mean a further drain on government funds. This lack of logic in criticism on the part of our opponents bespeaks either bad faith or incompetence.
By expounding contradictory, self-demolishing theories, Liberal members are showing to the whole country that they have been unable to conceive a genuine and realistic economic policy.
Already, on previous occasions, the Prime Minister has described to the house the fiscal policy devised by the government to ensure economic recovery, and he has clearly defined the three ways in which the Conservative government plans to fight unemployment.
On Friday June 6 the Prime Minister made a statement in this house which can be found on page 899 of Hansard for that day:
According to economists there are several means that should be adopted. One is to provide additional consumer monetary assistance in order that the consumer may be able, by the expansion of his income, to make purchases, thereby improving the general situation. The second is by a public works program. The third is by action in the reduction of taxes. All three courses of action have been followed. In no case has any one of these three legs of the tripod, as it were, for recovery been followed in its entirety. Each
The Budget-Mr. Morissette complements the other. None of the three by itself is recognized by economists as sufficient to meet the situation.
That is what the Conservative government has done. Its first move was to reduce taxes.
Since the election of June 10, 1957, the government has reduced taxation by a total sum of about $200 million. It has helped keep purchasing power at a high level by improving all forms of social security legislation. It raised the old age pension and allowances to the disabled and the blind. Its new fiscal concessions to provincial governments have allowed the Quebec legislative assembly, for instance, to increase in turn its allowances to needy mothers. It enacted repeated and numerous extensions to unemployment insurance legislation, in respect of seasonal benefits. Finally, to complete these two first steps, the government has set into motion a vast public works program.
Within the present day economic context, this federal government policy has proved both appropriate and timely. The economic situation is already improving, and we can infer from a number of factors that Canada's economic activity is again on the upgrade.
Consumer demand is growing at a satisfactory and steady rate. The employment index is rising.
According to the national employment service, in May 1958 the national labour force was 6,031,000, as against 5,881,000 in May 1957. That is an increase of 150,000 over last year. Prospects for the home building industry were never so good. This is a direct consequence of the government's generous and bold policy in this matter.
As the Minister of Finance pointed out in his budget speech, in the first four months of the present year the number of building starts were 80 per cent greater than for the same period in 1957. Many facts point to the growing stability and buoyancy of Canadian economy. Home building activity recently went up 15 per cent over last January. I have already noted that with regard to the corresponding period of last year, that increase is of the order of 80 per cent.
The price of the industrial securities registered in the stock market, I mean common shares, are two to three per cent higher than at the beginning of the year. Commercial and industrial construction was more active in March and April. The weekly averages of hours of work in manufactures show new
1712	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Morissette firmness as do wholesale prices in the field of industrial production. Finally, our exports, one of the decisive factors of our national prosperity, have risen in March and April.
According to the Federal Bureau of Statistics, the total volume of our exports represented, in March 1957, the sum of $361 million; in March 1958, the corresponding figure was $369 million. In April 1957, the figure was $365 million and, in April 1958, it had reached $371 million.
It is easy to forecast that, as the economic activity improves in other countries, especially in the United States, Canada's export position should improve further.
It is reassuring to think that the recession itself has been much less serious in Canada than in the United States. It is fair and reasonable to believe that the sole reason why the economic situation deteriorated much less in Canada than in the United States has been the wisdom of the financial and economic policy of the Conservative government.
In March 1958, the retail trade in the United States was 5.6 per cent below its level of July 1957. In Canada, the volume of retail sales has increased by 12 per cent from July 1957 to March 1958 and this trend seems to continue.
Industrial production went down 10 per cent in the United States from July 1957 to March 1958. In Canada, the difference is but 3.3 per cent.
New construction projects in the United States are just about beginning to reach the level of last year, while in Canada a very strong rising tendency has contributed to strengthen our economy substantially.
Instead of protesting vehemently, and of describing as outrageous the deficit forecast by the Minister of Finance, Liberals should remember that, before the June 1957 election, they failed to take the energetic measures which could have then warded off the recession. When the first symptom of an economic slowdown became apparent, the Liberals kept finding delight in a stupid inflationary intoxication. Not until a Conservative government took power were adequate and appropriate measures taken to deal efficiently with a disturbing slackening of economic activity.
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed strange to hear Liberals rejecting today, as a matter of political expediency, the economic creed they had professed at one time.


Even since John Maynard Keynes wrote his very famous "General theory of employment, interest and money", in 1935, the Liberals have claimed to be die-hard "Keynesians". It can be said, Mr. Speaker, that certain economists, great advisers of the Liberal party, have never been ashamed to confess candidly that they had been fana-ticized and bewitched by the great English economist. They have always claimed to be the champions of a cyclical tax policy. But when, in 1958, a Conservative government introduces a budget which, precisely, has due regard for all that is best in contemporary economic thinking, the Liberals heap abuse upon it. I say, Mr. Speaker that this attitude enlightens us on the score of their inconsistency or lack of sincerity.
If the Liberals were sincere and if they wanted to be consistent, they would congratulate the Minister of Finance and the Conservative government for having the courage to accept all the liabilities of a deficit budget at a time when everyone knows that it is the best and perhaps the only way to cope efficiently with the recession and to establish in Canada a full employment economy.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I wish to deal briefly with a few matters concerning my constituency.
First of all, I take pleasure in thanking the government, since the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) announced on June 6, when we were discussing the estimates of his department, that he intends to spend a sum of approximately three million dollars for the construction of a winter harbour at Father's Point. I am happy at the thought that work will start this very year. This year-round boat service linking the area with the north shore will alleviate the present isolation on that shore and help reduce the great cost due to seasonal ups and downs in our economy. When we think, Mr. Speaker, that, all along the 700 miles from the mouth of the Saguenay to the Atlantic, the people and industry on the north shore rely only on navigation for their supplies and the shipping of all kinds of products, we can easily grasp how much this project will help develop the area and promote the welfare of local residents.
Following the example of my friend, the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. English) I also would emphasize the necessity of extending the railway from Matane to Ste. Anne des

Monts. The Gaspe peninsula needs this link between its raw materials and the markets. An extension such as this would do much to increase prosperity along the lower St. Lawrence and in Gaspe peninsula.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw the government's attention, and especially that of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) to a problem of acute import to my constituency at the moment: that of air navigation. My constituency has two airports: one at Rimouski and the other at Mont Joli. The one at Mont Joli was built during World War II and involved the investment of about $20 million, but, unfortunately, is practically out of use today. In the last few years, under the Liberal administration, no active step was taken to bring it back to its former status. By their geographical location, facing the north shore-now in full-geared activity, as a result of the development and operation of the iron ore deposits in the Quebec-Labrador area-the airports of Rimouski and Mont Joli occupy a strategical position.
I ask the government to consider whether it would be possible, by improving and modernizing those airports, to stimulate air transportation in my area. At any rate, it is absolutely necessary from the economic point of view in the area of the lower St. Lawrence and of the constituency of Rimouski that strong steps be taken in order that our airports may obtain part of the air traffic which the development of the Ungava and new Quebec has created and will continue to create.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would also like to say to the voters of the constituency of Rimouski how grateful I am to them for the eloquent tribute of confidence they gave me on March 31 by electing me to represent them in the parliament of our nation, with the greatest majority-barring a single exception-ever granted a member for Rimouski. My only ambition is to serve humbly in the defence and promotion of the rightful interests of my electors. I believe that by working for the prosperity of our own particular home constituency, we are all working here for the prosperity of this great homeland of ours, our beloved country, Canada.
The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Che-vrier) had words of regret, the other day, for the position of Quebec Conservatives. My hon. friend is at present a victim of a frustration complex. I am pleased to say to him that we, Conservative members from 57071-3-109

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would be very remiss indeed if I did not offer my congratulations to my old and good friend from Hamilton South (Mr. McDonald) for the speech he delivered a while ago. I have always felt that the hon. member for Hamilton South, and I say this without any fear of contradiction whatsoever, was one of the greatest footballers Canada ever developed. He not only brought a great deal of honour to himself, his family and the city of Hamilton but also to the big four football organization. I must confess that many times I sat with the other fans in Hamilton and cheered him lustily for his good playing, little realizing at that time that I was cheering a Tory.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I must say that he brought
honour to himself and was a perfect gentleman on the football field as he is in the House of Commons.
For a few minutes I should like to deal with something not particularly connected with the budget but first of all may I congratulate the previous speakers who over the course of the last five or six days have argued the pros and cons of the budget. At this time I should like to discuss some of the problems with regard to what I consider is a very troublesome, perplexing and not well understood tax, the income tax. I was quite impressed on reading a statement of Mr. W. M. F. Petry, a noted archaeologist who made a study of the rise and fall of nations and civilizations which gave him unusual insight into the outcome of man's experiments with government. He made the statement that democracies consume themselves through excessive and unjust taxation until they collapse and are succeeded by men on horseback or the rank growth of the jungle.
Representative William Cockran of New York years ago warned that democratic institutions must perish from the face of the earth if they cannot protect the fruits of

The Budget-Mr. Houck human industry wherever they are or in whatever proportion they may be held by the citizens.
I think we have failed fully to realize that through our tax system we have been playing right into the hands of the Marxists who gleefully hail the income tax as the one sure instrument that will bring capitalism to its knees. We also have failed utterly to see that communism is not a political philosophy or plan but rather is a state of impotence to which those marked for subjugation by would-be dictators must be, and are, reduced in order to assure absence of effective resistance. But there are other reasons for taking a dim view of our tax system, particularly the income tax, that are no less urgent than the fact that the system has become an ideological bombshell.
I could mention people in many categories whose skill and talents have placed them in the higher brackets, yet the taxes that they have to pay are certainly brutal. I think the professional athlete fares about as badly as anyone. If one is fortunate enough to break through to the top he usually does well income-wise, but the way up is pitifully unrewarding, so much so that those who make the grade more often than not mount the throne of glory head over heels in debt and their reign usually is short. These are the people with whom the tax collecter forms a real heads I win tails you lose partnership. Even the people with a regular earning power are by no means the only sufferers from our income tax laws. Almost everybody now has been gathered under the tent and the percentage of those taxed leaves few immune to plucking who have enough feathers to notice.
It is my belief that one of the strongest and most serious counts in the indictment against the income tax is its complexity. It certainly started out simple enough, but I do not think it is an exaggeration to say that it has become as frustrating, confusing and bewildering a fiscal problem as the Canadian people ever had to cope with. I certainly give the department credit for trying everything they could think of to make this tax understandable, and it is my belief they have made some progress. Relatively few people can handle even the short form or T1 general tax return without assistance. Naturally, the forms have to follow the law. They cannot be made any simpler than the law, and anyone who cannot understand the law cannot very well be expected to understand the form. It certainly is an unhappy truth that it seems to be impossible to have simplicity and fairness at the same time.

Most of the complexity in the present law came from efforts to plug the so-called loopholes and remove discrimination. Let no one assume that the income tax law is any better understood in official circles than it is by its lay victims. This honourable house is not made up of supermen or superwomen. It is simply a collection of human beings like everybody else and I hope no one will think that I wish to make any attack on these people, but to be perfectly frank I must suggest that just as no one has to understand what dynamite is made up of to know that it can blow a person to kingdom come, so no member or parliament or senator has to know how to determine the tax consequence of intricate corporate reorganizations to have found out by now that the income tax is hopelessly complicated and a Trojan horse.
May I ask this question? Who, if anybody, does really understand this tax? How about the people who write it? The answer is not greatly different. By the time the tax branch and their staffs get through with the grist that is delivered to their mills, many undecipherable changes have been wrought. The problem then presented is well illustrated by the struggle the experts in the treasury department have been having with the job of getting out regulations to cover the code. It isn't that the people in the treasury department and the national revenue service have not been trying to get these regulations to be clearly understood; quite the contrary, I think they have been knocking themselves out at it. But it has been extremely difficult for them to reach agreement as to just what the government means at many points and equally difficult to agree on how to express the intentions of the government after they have agreed upon what the intentions were.
Honest and efficient administration of public affairs cannot be achieved by invasion of the prerogatives and assumption of the responsibilities of executive officials by legislative bodies, committees, individuals or committee staffs. I have never believed that enduring honesty or efficiency can be achieved by legislation. Honest and official public administration can be achieved only by honest and efficient administrators, honestly appointed and free to act only in the interest of the people.
Another count in the indictment against the income tax, and a very serious one, is the cost of it. There are two categories of this cost: (1) what the government spends to administer the law; and (2) what the taxpayer pays to comply with it. In identifying the first category, the cost, I did not speak of it as a cost which the government pays. The government does not pay any part of

this cost. The taxpayers pay every cent of it, the cost of administration as well as the cost of compliance. The government never pays anything. It spends, and the taxpayer pays. I am not suggesting that the revenue service is wasteful or inefficient, because I know better. What I am suggesting is that the complexity of the income tax law necessitates the use of a lot more people in our nation's revenue department than would be necessary under a simple and better understood revenue system, and that therefore the cost of administration is a great deal more than it ought to be. We continually hear complaints from the revenue department, and I think it is the irony of the present situation, that they do not have enough on the staff to assure adequate enforcement. Sometimes I think we have more fear that the taxpayer would react adversely to close enforcement of the law than concern about the revenue that would be lost by inadequate enforcement. I have never felt that people resent full enforcement of tax laws. They do resent inadequate enforcement because they well know that a lot of people do not pay what they should when enforcement is inadequate.
Many taxpayers have complained bitterly to me about this situation, and sometimes I think the gentlemen who are acting in the tax department assume the role, and improperly, so, that because of the fact they are like an officer whose coat is filled with brass buttons, they assume too much authority and demand too much of the taxpayer. I have a case in point in my own riding where the tax men went to a doctor's home and demanded to see not only his will but his wife's will, and they broke the seal upon both of these wills, and kept this doctor's books for a year-and-a-half without returning them. This sort of action breeds a feeling of ill-will against any government.
Many taxpayers have complained bitterly to me, and I am sure to many members of this honourable house about this sort of situation and I must admit I cannot honestly disagree with them. All I could do, like any other member, was to try to explain the problem in my meagre way and beg their indulgence. No one ever refused to listen to me, but none of them were happy about it and I do not blame them.
If a satisfactory substitute for the income tax cannot be found, the only answer to the first complaint is more revenue agents of top grade, but I must be frank in saying that I doubt if this government or any other government would permit the service to have all the agents it needs. I think some of the members of this house must fear what many knowing outsiders firmly believe, namely that 57071-3-109i
The Budget-Mr. Houck if this House of Commons allowed the revenue service to have enough money for all-out enforcement of the income tax the demand for repeal would become so great within a year that it would be irresistable.
Another count in the indictment is that the income tax is unstable, being based upon income. It is a low producer in slack times and the high producer when times are good. Thus, theoretically, rates must be raised when people are least able to pay, and may be lowered when everybody is most able to pay.
The man-made deficiencies of the income tax laws are to a large extent the consequences of submission to the demands of pressure groups. For instance tremendous accumulations of income producing wealth have been removed from the jurisdiction of the income tax law by the exemptions granted to foundations and certain other nonprofit organizations about which I am not complaining. I think these exemptions are perfectly justified, are right and should be continued. What I object to is the fact that billions of dollars of potential income also are kept out of reach of the tax collector by government's engagement in business activities that compete with private enterprise.
Too much has been done deliberately to keep taxable income from keeping pace with economical development and growth, thus precluding realization of the full potentialities of the income tax as a revenue producer and making it more and more unequal to its job.
With the income tax having proven to be an unstable source of revenue I think the government has availed itself of a variety of other taxes. Some, if not many, of these taxes could be dispensed with if the primary tax were a stable one and could be permitted to produce fully and freely.
Naturally hon. members are going to ask themselves the question: What can be done about all this? I suggest to hon. members of this house that the time has come to take a new and critical look at our whole tax system. After all, some elements of the present tax system seem to be as old as our dominion itself.
Naturally age alone is not a sufficient reason to condemn any particular tax or any part of our tax system, but to me there is a lot more wrong with the income tax besides its age. Naturally, you are going to ask me-and rightly, what I would suggest to remedy this serious situation. My proposal would be a simple one. It is that this house appoint a commission-type group to make a really critical analysis of the income tax in particular and other tax systems in general and to study such reasonable proposals as

The Budget-Mr. Houck may be made with regard to both. I think such a study is long overdue. We have failed in the past but there does not seem to be much of a search for anything better and this search could be conducted on a continuing basis. Research pays off handsomely for business as to matters far less important to it than the government's tax system. It is time the government got some research started in this important field. Such a commission as I have in mind should be a non-partisan one and all the responsibility for it and its findings should be assumed by this House of Commons. Moreover, it should not be put under the handicap of a deadline. It should have time to do a thorough job and not be restricted in any way in its enquiry.
Then again I know that hon. members will ask me the question, "Well, what if we get rid of the income tax what would you put in its place?" That is a fair question but to me that is not the immediate problem. The necessity for a commission to go into the whole problem of taxation thoroughly would be lost in an argument whether or not mine or your suggestions would be feasible. Those who have vested interest in maintaining the status quo would see to that. There are many such people and I must admit some of them have tremendous political power. For the time being I must content myself by saying that I believe that a law or system can be contrived that would be simple enough for the average taxpayer to understand. Such a system might be relatively inexpensive for the government to administer and the taxpayer to comply with and at the same time be a stable source of revenue. Certainly such results have been worked out in many cases in very important categories of business enterprise. I believe that the same can be worked out for business generally and for individuals as well.
I say to the hon. members of this house that there is not any time to lose. Whether you believe it or not, everybody is being overtaxed, the middle class is being taxed out of existence and the nation thereby is being robbed of its surest guarantee of continued sound economical development and growth and its staunchest bulwark against the rise of socialism. The marvels of television brought the truth home to us with indelible clarity. Certainly the big surprise to me and others as well has been how little we have left after the "gimme" man has taken his cut.
Too many people today do not have enough money left in their business after taxes are paid to keep them abreast of the demands of their customers and since even more is extracted from us as individuals we just do

not seem to accumulate anything and are not able to increase our investment in our businesses, or in our country's growth. I repeat and with emphasis indeed that things are mighty serious largely because of the tax system and the income tax. Big business gets bigger and little business and substantial middle class folks are beginning to disappear. We were concerned about the future because we did not believe we could stand another serious recession. High rates of tax certainly could not mean anything when we have not anything to tax.
May I say again that time's a-wasting and the enemies of the way of life that we cherish so greatly rejoice as we are led closer and closer to national suicide. So I leave this question to hon. members of the house: What are we going to do about it? Let us do something about it before it is too late.
Mr. C. W. Hodgson (Victoria, Onl.k Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate I first want to congratulate the Speaker, yourself and the chairman of committees. This is my first opportunity to do so since you three have taken office. I want to say that in the discharge of your duties you are doing a wonderful job, to the honour of this chamber and yourselves, in maintaining the traditions and the dignity of parliament.
Next I want to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker)-and this also is my first opportunity to do that-on the wonderful majority he has brought into this house for the benefit of Canada through the Conservative party. He has carried on and won two campaigns within a year. Some hon. members say: "Oh, he had good candidates". It is true that he had good candidates; but I want to say that it is much easier to get good candidates under the leadership of John Diefenbaker. He talked the same talk and the same politics in Vancouver and Newfoundland and Ontario as he did in Quebec.

Never mind, John, you are doing all right. The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) said, as recorded at page 916 of the Hansard for the same date:
One of the points that I believe was dear to the heart of the hon. member for Victoria, Ont., when he was a critic in this particular field was that the trans-Canada highway was not wide enough, that the 22 foot strip led to a concentration and a wearing out of the highway so that by the time the project is completed the highway is going to be in a state of needing rebuilding. He made the point very well, I thought, that a broader highway-even a 24 foot highway-would be to the best advantage. I should like to have some word on how he has gotten along in his work within the department in seeing that this is coming to pass.
One of the other things in connection with the trans-Canada highway was this. I noticed there seems to be a popular clamour from new Conservative members in Alberta and Saskatchewan to have a second trans-Canada highway instituted under the general overlordship of the federal government.
I would suggest to the minister that in certain parts of Canada we are still waiting for the trans-Canada highway itself to be completed, and that before he follows this rush of enthusiasm from the west he should begin taking steps to get the provincial governments working much faster on completing the highway as it is. I wonder whether
1718	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Hodgson if in this regard he would consider offering Premier Frost of Ontario some sort of bonus in order to get his department of highways working a little harder up in northwestern Ontario.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member would permit a question. Would he tell us whether, when he becomes minister of public works, he will pay 90 per cent of the cost of the trans-Canada highway?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think I will be perfectly safe in promising that, because I have to become a minister first. However, I would like to say to the hon. member that if there was any special concession given to Ontario his group would foe the first to holler to high heaven.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We would like it for Newfoundland.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
After all, this government has a mutual understanding with all the provinces and they must all be treated in the same way. As far as the 22-foot strip is concerned, in some places where the highway is taken over from the provincial highway it is only 20 feet wide and in some places 22 feet. But as soon as we became the government there were negotations from an engineering standpoint between the provincial and federal governments. We have been in favour of building a 24-foot highway but, after all, the wishes of the provinces must be considered and in connection with the procedure in the province of Ontario we have put a 22-foot hard top on the trans-Canada highway and where a piece of provincial highway was taken over where the road was only 20 feet wide, all the grading and work done since is prepared for a 24-foot top. I might say that all the pavement in connection with the trans-Canada highway being laid this year in the province of Ontario will have a 24-foot top.
The hon. member for Port-Arthur made reference to the width of the trans-Canada highway and suggested a bonus for the province of Ontario for the early completion of the highway and I think he has been answered.	The provisions of the trans-
Canada highway agreement permit a minimum of 22 feet and a maximum of 24 feet pavement. This government would prefer all of the highway to be 24 feet. In Ontario, however, they had in some sections elected to complete to the 22-foot width. There have been discussions with provincial officials at the engineering level and it is our understanding that they are prepared to build the new construction to the 24-foot width. This point is being pushed by the department.


With reference to progress in Ontario, the work is being pushed. We have received from the province a very tight construction schedule which they have prepared to complete the paved highway on the route by 1960.
A particular effort is being made in the gap section from Agawa to Marathon, a distance of 165 miles. All grading contracts will be awarded by July of this year and it is proposed to award paving contracts for 45 miles before the end of the year. To date, $10,537,000 has been spent on the gap and another $12 million is estimated to be spent this year.
Mr. Speaker, I have some figures covering commitments on the estimated cost of construction of the trans-Canada highway for the fiscal years 1956-57 and 1957-58 and then the payments to the provinces in connection with the additional 40 per cent contribution to the cost of construction as provided for under section 6 (1) b and section 6 (1) c of the trans-Canada highway agreement. Then there are figures concerning the paving mileage approved and completed under the agreement. I have recently received these figures and would like to have them appended to my speech as part of Hansard.

There is one other matter I would like to bring to the attention of the house and that is the occasion when my name was again brought into the discussion, this time by the hon. member for Levis as reported at page 912 of Hansard of June 6, 1958 when he said:
At this point I should also like to ask-the hon. member for Victoria (Ont.) also inquired about this some years ago-if the minister has made any approach to the government of the province of Quebec so as to convince them to share in this program if it is not too late.
All I could say about that is that there has been a certain amount of ill will between the government of the province of Quebec and the federal government for a number of years. I believe the election of June 10, 1957, and the election of March 31, 1958, ended a lot of that disagreement and misunderstanding and I think there is now a better feeling between the federal government and all the provinces than there has been for a number of years. I hope the provinces and the federal government will strengthen their good will and understanding because the provinces and the federal government must be united if we are to have a united Canada and there must be a maximum of understanding and co-operation between them.
The hon. member for Port Arthur was heard from again on June 6 and we find his remarks recorded at page 913 of Hansard of that date. He had this to say:
One of the points I wanted to bring up was that two years ago the hon. member for Victoria (Ont.) made an interesting comment during the consideration of these estimates. He said something like this:
Last year, I made some reference to patronage. So long as you do something for my riding, I do not care how much patronage you use. So long as we get a little project, a building here and there, we shall be satisfied. The little bit of patronage that is used by the department at times does gripe a little, but never mind we shall stand the gripes if the minister will get busy.
I said that two years ago and I said it a year ago and I still say it now, as far as that is concerned.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What did the hon. member say about patronage?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As far as I was concerned I meant it for my own riding. I did not say it about any other riding. If the Liberals wanted to use a little patronage in my riding it did not affect me very much nor did it affect the C.C.F. because neither the Liberal or C.C.F. party got any more votes. All the votes the C.C.F. got could be put in your hip pocket. That is how the few pieces of paper were involved. Whatever patronage the Liberals might have used in my riding it did not affect the Liberal vote either because I kept getting more Liberal votes all the time. I had to have 5,000 Liberal votes to get the
The Budget-Mr. Hodgson majority I did. Why should I object to a Liberal receiving a job through Liberal patronage? The chances are he was voting for me in any event. I can understand that the C.C.F. would be worried about it because they did not get enough votes to amount to anything. But I will say this about the C.C.F., they are courageous people. They run a candidate every election.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why don't you give him a job?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He is a good fellow and he does not need one. He is not as poor as some of the members of the C.C.F. would have us believe they are when they are howling about it all the time. This chap can look after himself financially and otherwise but it does not assist him in getting votes.
The hon. member for Port Arthur went on to say:
This, of course, raises a nasty suspicion in my mind that perhaps patronage did exist in the Department of Public Works under this nefarious regime which ended last June. We righteous people are worried, because of the approach of the member who has been parliamentary assistant to that department, as to whether or not patronage still exists. This suspicion was increased last session when the minister, in answer to a question from a gentleman on the Liberal benches who has since moved to a more exalted realm in Quebec, suggested that the building of certain river improvements was more likely to have been placed in certain areas if the people in the area happened to be good Liberals. As I say, these suspicions are going around in our minds. We are prepared to accept that the new minister is a very forthright and very honest individual. He has made a number of public statements that no such thing as patronage is going to exist. I feel, therefore, he should be prepared now to make a statement about the patronage he found in the department and the steps he has taken to stamp it out. Certainly, he should say what steps he has taken to watch his erstwhile parliamentary assistant who said he did not care how much patronage there was as long as his riding got a little bit. Now that may be in keeping with the free enterprise ethics we heard stated so well yesterday. However, it seems at odds with the minister's own position, and we would like to hear more about that.
There is one more aspect of patronage I should like to mention, and this has come to the notice of those on the opposition benches. There are not many defeated Conservative candidates across Canada, and I know that makes a number of people around this chamber very happy. Those few defeated Conservative candidates that do exist have, in a few instances since the last election, come out with statements in their local papers. These statements seem to have been triggered by letters they received from the Department of Public Works or officials of that department to the effect the government, in its graciousness, is going to do something here or there. In other words, we have defeated Conservative candidates announcing government projects as a result of what seems to be a pipe line into the Department of Public Works.
From my knowledge of the Department of Public Works there is no pipe line into the
1722	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Hodgson department that is not open to all members of parliament. If any hon. member wants to establish a pipe line into the Department of Public Works all he has to do is write a letter to the department setting out what he wants to know and he will receive the information without any trouble.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member who is presently waiting in the outer courts to be called as a parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Public Works permit a question? When he or other persons notify the defeated Conservative candidate of a proposed public works in the riding is the sitting member for the riding, if he happens to be in opposition, also notified?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Turning now to another subject-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is the answer?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I did not catch the hon. member's question. I thought he was making a speech.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Make it simple.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When a Conservative candidate for any constituency is notified by some person in the Department of Public Works that any certain public works project is going to be undertaken in his riding is the sitting member for the riding, if he happens to be an opposition member, also notified at the same time?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I cannot tell you that. I only know that if any hon. member wishes to receive information from the Department of Public Works he has only to write in to obtain it. The department consists of a fine group of civil servants who are very cooperative. I do not think they have any politics. My personal experience with the department indicates that they are always open and above board in all their dealings.
I could continue to quote passages from the remarks made by the hon. member for Levis but I do not think it is necessary. He is a nice little fellow and I will say this to you about him. The hon. member for Levis had a lot more authority with the Department of Public Works than I do to either hire or fire.
The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Che-vrier) also expressed an interest in the business of patronage and his remarks can be found at page 1137 of Hansard of June 13. I might note that at one point he made reference to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) although I believe he intended to refer to the hon. member for Port Arthur. Apparently the Liberals are interested in patronage too and I think the hon. member for Laurier was more or


less setting traps. I must point out that he was not a very good trapper because he did not catch the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) in any of the traps he set; at least he did not succeed in having the minister make whatever statements he might have been interested in having him make.
I wish to deal briefly with one of the statements made by the hon. member for Port Arthur as found at page 914 of Hansard which I have already placed on the record when he said:
Certainly, he should say what steps he has taken to watch his erstwhile parliamentary assistant who said he did not care how much patronage there was as long as his riding got a little bit.
I must confess that I was not aware that the parliamentary assistant had any authority that would warrant his being watched very carefully but I was interested in the remarks of the erudite hon. gentleman from the Lake-head and so I looked up in the dictionary the meaning of the word "erstwhile" to ascertain exactly what it means. According to Webster's dictionary it means "before" or "before long".

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are the last two words a prayer?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are becoming a good scholar.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Take that for what it is worth. So far as patronage is concerned, this government does not know anything about it, at least I do not think they do. They are babes in the woods compared with the former Liberal government.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about Mr. Carson Stroud?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
So far as patronage is concerned, they are babes in the woods. I know this from what happened in my riding. I do not have to go across Canada. The hon. member for Laurier was minister of transport for a number of years. In the letting out of jobs or in the hiring of people his party and his department were rife with patronage right in my own riding. There was nothing I could do about it. I can well remember when I got a little money from the government to build a dock in a place called Bobcaygeon. What happened? Talk about pipe lines. In the Department of Public Works and in the Department of Transport, and you can also add in the department of the post office, there is such a thing as appointing foremen and inspectors. The present government puts these jobs out for competition. Under the old government there was no competition. Who was the inspector on the first job that was done in my riding after I became elected in 1945? Was it a Liberal,

a Conservative or a C.C.F.'er. No, it was the humble defeated Liberal candidate, the man whom I defeated and who was a member of this house for 10 years. He was the inspector. On the next job on Cameron lake the next year, who was the inspector? It was the same individual and that sort of thing went on. There never was a competition run for the job of inspector at any time under their regime in my riding. So far as the Department of Public Works and the post office are concerned, the same thing took place there.
There was a competition once for a postmastership in Bobcaygeon. This is the way the competition was run. The district postmaster at Toronto came up to Bobcaygeon and he talked to the heads of the Liberal association there. They went over to a garage and got a little fellow out of the garage, a nice little boy, and he turned out to be a good postmaster, too. He was installed and the old gentleman was retired. That is how the competition worked. I happened to be the member and some people did not like what happened and they were bothering me about another fellow who wanted the job. So I took it upon the floor of the house with the postmaster general and they had a competition. The competition was held in June. Although the other fellow had some months experience in the post office, the second man had five years overseas experience and six years experience in the army. He won the competition on both the written and oral examination. He had four years of high school and one year in college. What happened? Did he get the job? He got a large form from the civil service commission. We have the form framed if anybody wants to see it. The form stated that he had won the written and oral examination by so many marks, and so on, and that his appointment would be made early in September.
July went by, August went by and September came. September went by and there was no appointment. The people began bothering their member of parliament again. I got on my horse and I drove down to Ottawa and low and behold the postmaster general would not see me. I could not get on to his plush carpets; I could not see him. Of course, the girl asked me what I was there about. I said I wanted to talk about the postmastership at Bobcaygeon. I could not get in to see him. I started calling him on the telephone and after six or eight calls he talked to me about it. He said that the other fellow had three, four or five months experience and he did not think it right to turn him out. So the minister overruled the decision of the
27, 1958
The Budget-Mr. Boulanger civil service commission. That is the way patronage was played in my riding from that day until June 10, 1957.
Patronage permeated other departments besides the Post Office Department. It was as bad in the Department of Public Works and in the Department of Transport while the hon. member for Laurier was minister of transport. In my riding I have from 165 miles to 240 miles of the Trent canal and waters and lakes. There are 25 or 30 men hired temporarily every spring and two or three permanent men retired every year and new ones hired. Never once did a Conservative get a job on the Trent canal; in fact, a Conservative can hardly look into the canal. After I was elected for a year I thought it was about time that the houses occupied by the workers on the canal were wired. I was down near the canal one day and I thought I would drive down and see what was going on. I drove over to the canal and got out. Instead of walking all around as I should have done I walked across the locks. I got half way across the locks when a man came out screaming, "Get off there, get off there". He came over to the locks. I thought every man in my riding knew me, but I found out that one fellow did not because I said, "I am the Conservative candidate". He said, "You get the hell out of here; you can't put that bull over me". He said, "There is no room for a Conservative around here, anyway". He is still on the job. I think he is a good lockmaster.
Then we have the Department of Trade and Commerce. They have a little patronage in there, too. They appointed some six or eight statisticians up in our country and again not one Conservative, not even a C.C.F.'er, got a chance at those jobs. The appointments were made by the Liberal association and they were hand-picked. They were not only Liberals, they were good Liberal workers both before and after they got the job and even up to the last election. They died awfully hard, but they still have their jobs. I do not believe in firing everybody high wide and handsome. I do not believe in firing people who are doing a good job just because some political mistakes were made by somebody higher up who should know better.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They have seen the light now.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You can lead a horse to water but you cannot make him drink. They will be just the same if they ever get back into power but they will not be back in power for a long, long time.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to take part in the discussion of the budget and to

The Budget-Mr. Boulanger express my personal position and the views of the voting population of that grand riding of Drummond-Arthabaska.
The first words of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in his budget speech, were the following:
I approach this task tonight in a spirit of deep humility and dedication in recalling, as did some of those who have preceded me in delivering their first budget speech, that this honour has fallen in times past to the lot of some very great Canadians.
It was indeed with humility that such a budget had to be submitted and no Canadian has ever presented such a pitiful one since confederation. As someone said before, no government has ever submitted a budget with as large a deficit in peacetime.
In submitting an explanation for his $648 million deficit budget, the hon. Minister of Finance has broken with a long Liberal tradition. As a matter of fact, since 1946, i.e. the year after the war, we have seen the public debt gradually decrease, except in the fiscal years 1954-1955, when our deficit was $147 million, and 1955-1956, when it reached $17 million. However, these slight deficits were compensated by a surplus of $272 million in the years 1955, 1956 and 1957.
On April 1, 1958, the national debt was estimated at 11 billion 48 million dollars, i.e. $649 per capita. However, this debt had been of 13 billion and 400 million dollars in 1946, or $1,100 for each man, woman and child in this country. Under the able guidance of the Hon. Mr. Abbott, who was minister of finance until 1952, the debt gradually decreased and continued to be paid off under the equally capable leadership of the Hon. Mr. Harris.
At the time several members of the Conservative party were loud in their criticism of these administrators. But the latter deserved the gratitude of every Canadian citizen. Whatever the area in which they may, at this time, exercise their activity, they deserve our gratitude and our sympathy.
Since the Conservatives came into power, what has happened? Whereas Mr. Harris' budget forecast a $152 million surplus for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1958, we have seen the present Minister of Finance, not only absorb this surplus in its entirety, but end the year with a deficit of $40 million, not even considering the $250 million which, according to the hon. gentleman, had been camouflaged by the Liberal party. This means that the government has added $542 million to administrative expenditures since it has come into power, though we are still as far as ever from the earthly paradise which it had promised us. You will remember the promises made during
[Mr. Boulanger.l
the election campaigns of 1957 and 1958. There was not one Conservative candidate who did not express shock at Liberal government surpluses. It was said that each family should be reimbursed the $120 it had paid over the year in surplus taxation. It was also stated that the excise tax on automobiles should be repealed, that our natural resources should be developed, that employment should be kept at a high level, etc.
If we look at the forecast made by the Minister of Finance last year, to the effect that there would be an $80 million surplus on March 31, 1958, and if we look at the evidence of a $39 million deficit which was confirmed last week, we can easily deduce that, projecting this error in like proportion, next year's deficit will be one billion dollars. The most striking feature of the budget under discussion is the flagrant contradiction between the figures provided by the Minister of Finance and the promises recently made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker).
He was not sparing of words when telling us that, without regard to cost, we should see to it that the economic life of this country be activated in order to create employment. Last year in his stillborn budget, he reduced taxation by $178 million, bringing about, in so doing, no improvement in the situation. It was during the few months that followed this reduction in taxation that we have seen the unemployment figure reach 860,000.
This year, this reduction in taxes is only of the order of $8 million. At that it will only benefit those who wish to make a gift of $10,000 to their wife and children, those too who will leave, at their death, an estate of $60,000 and less. Even Don Juans will not have to pay taxes on the flowers which they distribute right and left, thanks to the generosity of the Minister of Finance.
True, there have been some slight deductions in taxes on certain construction materials, agricultural and horticultural products, without forgetting eyeglasses and rat poison. But what real relief will all this bring to the working class and to the heads of large households?
With the exception of medicine bought on prescription, and of other treatments for chronic ailments, there is very little that the Minister of Finance can show in the way of real relief for the ordinary citizen of this country.
We have reason to say that Tory times are hard times.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame!

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Since Confederation, not
one Conservative government ever presented a sensible budget. Under the Liberal administration, a budget deficit of $648 million would have meant, if that amount had been applied to relieve the taxpayer, a reduction of $38 for each citizen of our country. If the same amount had been applied to increasing family allowances, Canadian families would be receiving $15 to $20 per child.
Yet, it was none other than the Prime Minister who said that Liberals were picking out of the pockets of every Canadian family $120 which the government did not need to administer the affairs of this country. When saying this, he was taking advantage of people's honesty in order to draw votes. The Canadian people were taken in and must now suffer the consequences, though with regret.
Mr. Speaker, I did not want to let the consideration of this budget go by without dealing with some aspects of family allowances. In fact, I received a great number of requests from citizens of my constituency asking me to urge an increase in family allowances. There is no doubt that all members in this house have received such requests.
These requests are fully justified by the increase in the cost of living and by the ever-pressing needs of education.
In January 1957, on the basis of the rise in the cost of living, the Liberal government understood and raised family allowances at the same time it raised old age pensions, pensions to the needy and all other social welfare benefits. A few months later, it was the Conservative government which, immediately after taking power, increased the old age pension by $9 a month, for the same reasons, while forgetting about family allowances. It is strange to find that the Conservatives who gave themselves as champions of social justice did not apply the same principles to the protection of the family.
One would have to look into the hearts of the Tories to find the real reasons of their indifference towards large families.
Since the Hon. George Drew, former leader of the opposition, opposed family allowances in 1945, the Conservatives have consistently grumbled that the Liberals had gone beyond the limit to meet the demands of the people. Still recently, in 1956, at the Conservative convention, the party defined its stand when the Hon. G. I. Smith, to a lady who asked him what was the attitude of his party in that field, answered that the committee instituted to study that question did not feel able to recommend now an increase of family
The Budget-Mr. Boulanger allowances. On the other hand, the Liberal party, at its convention in January, did not hesitate to make its stand known and to add to its program the payment of family allowances to students up to the age of 18.
Today, the disproportion between old age pensions and family allowances is obvious and the Conservatives have substantially aggravated this lack of balance. At one time, we felt that the government would have decided on a certain increase in family allowances to meet the repeated demands of the population. Many members from the government side have therefore made statements in which they undertook to recommend such an increase. In fact, the Conservative members from the province of Quebec went all out, to their hearts' content, in their statements published in a certain paper of that province. Not one of them, however, had the courage to state squarely in this house what he desired. They have merely been using nice words, making no sense whatever. Yet, they are aware of the growing needs of large families with regard to maintenance and education.
The consumers' price index based on 100 for 1949-that is four years after the family allowances act was sanctioned-reached 125.2 in January last. The least the government could do at this session would be to continue to pay these allowances for children still pursuing their studies and until 18 years of age, and adjust pensions to a level comparing with old age pensions.
Any legislation that the government will introduce to improve that act will be welcomed by all citizens and there is no doubt that the Liberal party will approve it without reservation.
Mr. Speaker, before ending my remarks, I would be remiss if I did not say a few words about agricultural prices support. When that legislation was considered at the last session, there was much discussion and we were right, on the Liberal side, when we asked that its adoption should be delayed so that we could consider it further.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) was so anxious to have it adopted, so as to be able later to say that he had fulfilled one of his promises, that he did not care whether it would be detrimental or not to the farmers.
In the last few months, several reactions cropped up from many parts of the country. It is rightly claimed, for instance, that milk powder producers are affected directly, and the farmers indirectly. Those manufacturers are fairly numerous in the eastern part of the country, and especially in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec.

The Budget-Mr. Boulanger
Under the new price stabilization act, the Minister of Agriculture has decreed that the new prices would come into effect on May 1, 1958, and that the government was willing to pay 15 cents a pound for first quality dry skimmed milk, spray processed, and 12 cents a pound for roller processed dry skimmed milk.
Those new prices are 2 cents a pound less than those in force prior to May 1. Now, according to the figures of the Dried Milk Producers' Association, there were still in those plants, from 10 to 12 million pounds of milk powder. Those producers therefore took or will take a loss of 2 cents a pound when marketing their product. Those losses will account for $200,000. Some small manufacturers, whose financial situation is not too solid, will be in a very embarrassing situation.
If the government had at least announced its reduction policy a few months earlier, those producers would have had time to dispose of their stock.
A similar situation came about under the Liberal regime in the years 1942 and 1943. The government of the time paid a compensation to wholesalers who had quantities of butter in reserve when a price reduction was announced on this product. The butter producers, wholesalers and farmers were not then forced to sustain a loss and the change-over came about smoothly.
Since the reduction of the support price of dry milk by 2 cents per pound, the price of milk in Quebec and Ontario has been reduced by 10 cents per hundredweight. We know that approximately 8 pounds of dry milk can be obtained from approximately 100 pounds of milk plus 4.2 pounds of butter. By carrying out an extremely simple computation we will see that with the increase in the price of butter the profit is 4.2 cents per hundredweight. This shows that with regard to recent years butter has been selling for one cent more per pound, that is 64 cents. This increase, with regard to 100 pounds, is equal to a profit of 4.2 cents. If account is taken of the fact that 8 pounds of dry milk are produced from 100 pounds of whole milk, this decrease in 2 cents means a loss of 18 cents for the producer per hundredweight. By subtracting the loss incurred on dry milk production from the profit made on the sale of butter, we will note that the producer loses from 10 to 12 cents per hundredweight. What is happening at this time in the province of Quebec is that the price of butter has gone down from 10 to 12 cents per

hundredweight. And there is great praise for the agricultural prices production act which, according to some people, is the farmer's salvation!
We are still unable to see what the results of this act will be since it is far too recent; but we can state that this legislation, as far as milk products are concerned, is a complete failure from the point of view of the farmer. True, there are certain products in respect of which this legislation can be to some advantage for speculators or traders. This is true as far as wool is concerned. A compensation price of 60 cents a pound is being considered. Since this wool can be sold only to manufacturers or traders, the farmer is deprived of the advantage of bargaining and the manufacturer can offer him any price whatever. Whether the farmer sells his wool 40 cents, 50 cents, or 65 cents a pound is completely irrelevant since the government will pay the difference when the compensation price has been established on the basis of the price on the Toronto market. Therefore, if the compensation price is fixed at 60 cents and if the farmer has sold his wool at 40 cents, the government will pay the difference, that is 20 cents per pound. If that legislation has any advantage whatever, it is only as far as traders and manufacturers are concerned. Since the trader is not concerned with competition, he can offer any price he wishes. In fact, he can grade it in any way he chooses. I am convinced that there are no wool graders who really know anything about wool grading either in our Quebec manufacturing plants or among traders.
I had an opportunity to offer similar remarks last year, when we were discussing the Agricultural Prices Stabilization Act and I believe that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) will admit today that I was right.
We could deal with a great many other products, but I am content with noting these two, reserving the right to return to them later on.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, rising as I do now for the first time in this house, my first words must be of congratulation to the Speaker on the high office with which he has been honoured. It must be a source of great satisfaction to know that members of parliament from every party and every corner of the country were

not only pleased but proud to have him chosen again as the first commoner. We in this far corner of the House of Commons know that he will see us equally well and as often as he will see those members who are much closer to him. I should congratulate too, the hon. member for Longueuil (Mr. Sevigny) who has already demonstrated in this session that he will live up to the many fine things said about him by earlier speakers in this parliament.
St. Antoine-Westmount is a metropolitan Montreal riding about two miles and a half square. The 41,000 voters are a cross-section of Canadian life. Every walk of life, from the lowest to the highest, is represented. There are the very poor and the immensely wealthy. About half are French and the other half predominantly English. I will strive honestly to represent them all, not just those who voted Conservative in this parliament.
I might add that my constituents will be able to make a close and, 1 trust, friendly check on my activities here through the hon. member for Longueuil, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Chambers) and the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Keays), who are all residents of St. Antoine-W estmount.
I must record my approval of the budget presented to this house last Tuesday by the finance minister in a feat of endurance and easy speaking which I am sure was a marvel to all the new members like myself.
Naturally, I have been watching for and listening closely to all the comment available on the budget. I have been in my own riding of St. Antoine-Westmount this last weekend to hear the observations of my own constituents; and, notwithstanding what we have heard from certain sections of this house, I am forced to say that I believe most Canadians approve and are satisfied with this budget. Of course there is nothing in it to make anyone hysterical with joy. But there is an honest recognition of the facts of economic life in Canada as the people know them.
There was optimism, justifiable optimism, I believe for the future. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) has told us that this budget is only a first push to start the wheel turning forward. There is no reason not to believe that in subsequent budgets the wheel will gather momentum and that there will be the gradual, systematic reduction of taxes for which this party has always stood.
The Budget-Mr. Webster
Before discussing taxes at greater length, there is one feature of the budget and reaction to it which I think deserves some notice. We have heard repeated charges that this is a budget based on a protectionist philosophy. No doubt we will hear that claim made often even long after this budget has been approved here in parliament by the representatives of the people.
Some members of the opposition parties with whom we share this side of the House of Commons have found it convenient in their attack on the budget to quote the Financial Post, a paper with considerable standing in the business community. Let these critics, then, turn up page 10 of the Financial Post of June 21 where the tariff changes are discussed, and let them note these two paragraphs quoted from that article:
All of these changes-
The reference is to tariff revisions on iron and steel, pipes and tubes, zinc and zinc products and wool.
-are the result of tariff board investigations initiated under the Liberal government.
The Conservative government is following lines mapped out by its predecessor.
That ends the quotation and it should end too some of the fallacious arguments we have been hearing from other sections of the House of Commons about what these changes mean.
Before this diversion I was discussing taxes and the fact that I have found general approval of the budget in spite of the fact that there were no substantial tax reductions. The only people who seem really concerned about this are those sitting to your immediate left in the two opposition parties. They are in the minority in this house, and I am convinced they are still swimming against the stream of public opinion in the matter of this budget and other equally important questions. There was general agreement throughout the country even before the budget was presented *-and I am now not referring only to the events of March 31-that taxes should not be drastically reduced.
One of the most significant documents which came to my attention in the last few weeks was a copy of a letter from H. Roy Crabtree, chairman of the executive council of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. This organization is a national voluntary federation of more than 750 boards of trade and chambers of commerce in all Canadian provinces and the territories of the north as well. As such it represents literally thousands of businesses, large and small, who have as great a stake as you or I in every budget.
1728	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Webster
In January of this year the national chamber of commerce, visited the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) and urged upon them consideration of substantial reductions in personal and corporate income taxes. Four months later, however-in May-the executive council sought and received another interview with the Minister of Finance and his cabinet colleagues. The council felt it was important, in view of changed circumstances, to considerably amend its former position. During its first meeting the executive council had expressed the uncertainty that everyone felt at the time regarding the possible extent and duration of the adjustment which the Canadian economy was then undergoing. In May the chamber said, and I would like to quote from the letter to the ministers as follows:
There are still elements of uncertainty particularly as to the duration of the current slowdown in business. There is some recent evidence, however, of stabilizing tendencies.
The letter went on to discuss the fact that Canada's economy is directly affected by economic developments abroad, particularly those in the United States. It added that there appear to be what the chamber of commerce called feasible means of improving our economic climate through governmental and private policies designed to improve the confidence of business and consumer. Then the letter came to this significant conclusion:
During the intervening months-
That is, since the first submission made in January.
-the fiscal background has changed significantly. Having in mind the probable sizeable deficit of the government for the fiscal year ending March 31st, 1959, largely resulting from expanded spending to counteract prevailing unemployment, the executive council believes that it would not be prudent or responsible to recommend sizeable tax rate changes at this time.
I would like to repeat the last part of that important sentence.
-it would not be prudent or responsible to recommend sizeable tax rate changes at this time.
That is the considered opinion of the executive council of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. I do not think anyone could accuse that body of the political bias which inevitably flavours every speech made on this subject in this house. By the standards of this group the budget under discussion is, therefore, both prudent and responsible. Furthermore, the Minister of Finance apparently received similar advice from the large group of trusted and efficient officials in these departments which prepare studies to aid him in budget decisions.


Within this frame of reference, that is to say, "Hold the line on major tax cuts", the Minister of Finance has introduced some improvements which I am glad to hear, even the opposition admits, makes sound sense. The question must be lingering in many minds as to why these changes were not made by former governments. We have heard arguments that the welcome changes in deductions for medical expenses will be of very little value to very few people. I think this is an exaggeration because reduction of even a few dollars in tax payments is valuable to every Canadian affected. One argument is that the 3 per cent floor which must be exceeded in respect of medical expenses before all such expenses are deductible will severely limit the value of these changes. While medical charges are not altogether standardized, I think it is fair to say that it is much easier for a relatively low income family to run up 3 per cent of income in medical bills than it is for a higher income family to do so. These changes therefore will be of the most value to the Canadians who most need the benefits.
More and more Canadians are wearing eye glasses, and yet until the night of June 17, 1958 the federal government refused to accept the fact that weak eyes or any condition requiring eye correction was, for deduction purposes, a physical ailment.
The same is true of the bulk of drugs which are playing an increasingly important part in the treatment of illnesses. I imagine every member of this house knows of at least one case where the cost of drugs has been the largest item in the recovery of some patients. Laboratory and diagnostic services are also vital to the proper treatment of many ailments and, as I said earlier, it is only good sense that they should all be included for deduction purposes.
I could not agree more than I do with the statement of the Minister of Finance on this subject last week he told us of these changes, as recorded at page 1243 of Hansard for June 17 in the following words:
-will go a long way to correct the unfairness which in the past has been the source of so much complaint about this section of the income tax law.
The same words might apply to another change announced in the budget address. As every member must know, a wife could earn $999 without damaging the exemption which her husband could claim for her. But, as conditions were before the budget, if she earned $1,001 this exemption was immediately reduced by $250. I understand the change will eliminate this small but rather vicious anomaly. The deduction will now be reduced by only the exact amount of the wife's earnings in excess of $1,000.

The third announcement I would like to mention concerns the estate tax. A new bill was introduced in January last and since then many representations have been made. These representations we are told had resulted after careful consideration in a number of revisions. This proves to all concerned the wisdom of the course adopted by the house earlier this year in facilitating the introduction of this important legislation.
We have also been told that the tax relief envisioned by the new estate tax legislation is concentrated, deliberately, in the low value estates. Estates of less than $50,000 will be completely free from tax and widows will receive particular attention by means of a scale of exemptions which, as the minister explained, are true exemptions. In other words, the tax will be paid only on the amount by which the estate exceeds the total applicable exemptions.
In closing I would like to say the Minister of Finance is a Conservative, with both a large "C" and a small "c". If he has erred in any of his estimates and predictions forming part of his budget, his error has been on the side of caution. Therefore we have reason to believe that the situation will improve and that his controlled optimism will be more than justified.
I have spoken of the general policy decisions which had to be made in regard to this budget and I have mentioned three specific changes for which I am sure the majority of Canadians are grateful. I believe the points I have discussed underline my contention that this is a budget built on good sense. It is the kind of budget the people expected and that the country should have under the circumstances. I am therefore pleased to say that my vote against both amendments and for the main motion will be a vote for good sense more than a vote for political partisanship.
