speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 5 at the adjournment of the debate I was in the middle of a

sentence when, according to the report in Hansard, I was guillotined. During the interval of time I have had drawn to my attention an editorial appearing in a newspaper called the New Toronto Advertiser headed "Of Interest To Borrowers". I feel at this time I should read it in its entirety because to a large extent I feel there has been a matter of misrepresentation as far as I am personally concerned. The editorial reads as follows:
The people of Canada can consider themselves very fortunate that there is only one John Drysdale in the House of Commons. Because you have probably never heard of him, we will tell you that John Drysdale is the member for Burnaby-Richmond. His fleeting moment of fame or rather notoriety came this week during discussion on the C.C.F. motion to amend the Interest Act and limit interest to 12 per cent.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Order. May I call the attention of the hon. member to the practice that editorials which comment on proceedings in the house are not properly read in the course of debate.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
May I call the attention of Mr. Speaker to page 133 in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition, 1958, paragraph 7 which reads:
(7) When a complaint is made of a newspaper, it is the practice in the House of Commons of Canada for the member to rise on a question of privilege and point out that he has been libelled or misrepresented. He may read as much of the article as is necessary to prove his case but he cannot go farther. He is bound to confine himself strictly to the question of privilege.
On that point, Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege and ask for permission to read the editorial.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext: I understood the hon. member was speaking on the debate on second reading of the bill. He had not referred to any matter of privilege.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, during the interval this editorial appeared involving myself and in connection with the Interest Act. I am rising to speak following the adjournment and I wish to rise at the same time on a question of privilege. Being a new member I was not sure whether or not it was necessary under parliamentary procedure to raise a question of privilege but I do so now if it is necessary in order to read the editorial.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext: I have never heard of an hon. member interrupting himself to raise a point of privilege. The rules say a point of privilege may be considered at any time and it may be that the hon. member is right. If I have some advice on the subject I might give a better decision. Does any hon. member wish to speak on this question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I may address myself to the point, I think while the hon. member may be right in raising a question of privilege if he speaks now I do not think he will be able to get back to the subject which is under discussion because he cannot have it both ways. He cannot raise a question of privilege and interrupt his own speech and then go back and argue the resolution or bill which is now before the house. He must do either one or the other. He can raise the question of privilege before the orders of the day are called as any hon. member can but my submission is that he cannot have it both ways.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed to rise and bring up the question of privilege that the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Drysdale) wishes to interrupt himself on so as to transfer the liability from himself to me.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext: After I dispose of this point of order, I will consider it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I may offer to be of some help in resolving the dilemma. 1 listened very carefully to the hon. member and his remarks so far were only an introduction to what could be a question of privilege. I suggest that he could make his question of privilege now and later take part in the debate.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES

speechtext:
Thank you. I will not pursue the dilemma that I seem to be placing the house in at the present time. Perhaps I might paraphrase the effect of the editorial. The objection that I had to it primarily, sir, was that the length of the editorial is approximately the length of my interrupted speech and it ascribes to me certain points of view on the interest rate which I feel are inimical to the stand I took. The editorial continues by taking out certain phrases from the small speech that I made and then taking these particular phrases to back up or substantiate a preconceived conclusion that they had already reached. I felt it was extremely important, because the matter is of a great deal of interest to the people in my riding and to the people of Canada generally, and when a point of view is ascribed to me, to which I do not adhere, as stated in the

Interest Act
editorial, I feel that I should take the opportunity of clarifying the matter.
In substance the editorial adopts the attitude that the 12 per cent rate of interest is quite justifiable. At the beginning I pointed out to the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) that I agreed with the objective of the bill but I had great difficulty in ascertaining where he obtained the 12 per cent figure. These are some of the phrases used by the hon. member in 1957, as reported at page 1897 of Hansard, in reference to the 12 per cent rate:
Certainly loans made by the chartered banks to a great many credit unions in the country, money loaned under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the National Housing Act or the Canadian Farm Loan Act, all carry lower rates of interest.
He meant lower rates than 12 per cent. He went on to say:
I believe the terms of the bill are moderate. I think the suggested rate of 12 per cent per year is certainly as high as any rate should be.
Another reason why I suggest that rate is that many credit unions in Canada charge a rate of approximately that amount.
That is the only positive statement he made as to how the 12 per cent rate was established. Again, speaking on the same bill on January 10, 1958, at page 3164 of Hansard, the hon. member said:
The 12 per cent interest rate provided in this bill is, I think, high. Some hon. members on previous occasions have said that the rate should be lower and I think a good argument could be made in this respect, but this rate was proposed because it seemed to me that it was so reasonable that very few hon. members could oppose it.
Again, arguing in the debate on June 5, 1958, as reported at page 858 of Hansard, the hon. member said:
I do not think it can be successfully argued that a rate of interest should be in excess of 12 per cent per annum. As a matter of fact, I think 12 per cent is itself rather high but I have placed the ceiling in that amount in order to appeal to hon. members to do something about this problem.
In other words, the analogy, or the idea, that the hon. member for Assiniboia uses to establish the basis is that he looks on the credit unions as establishing the rate of 12 per cent. However, I would like to refer to the report of the royal commission on cooperatives in 1945, and specifically appendix E, which starts at page 239 and deals with the development and operations of credit unions-caisses populaires-in Canada, and in particular at page 242:
A credit union (caisse populaire) may be defined as an incorporated group of people with some well defined tie of association, occupation or residence, who pool their savings in the form of shares and deposits and out of the fund so accumulated, make loans to members only for purposes which are considered to be provident or productive.
The affairs of a credit union are administered by three committees appointed by and from the

members, namely, a board of directors, a credit committee and a supervisory committee.
The board of directors must rule on all applications for membership, each application being endorsed by at least one director. In addition, the directors determine the maximum individual share holding and the maximum individual loan which may be made with or without security, subject to the provisions of the act, determine interest rates on loans and deposits, declare dividends: (subject to the approval of the general meeting); have charge of investments, other than loans to members; fix the form and amount of security of officers and employees handling money; and fill vacancies on the board of directors or of the credit committee until the next annual meeting.
The legislation requires the credit committee to pass on all loans and determine the rate of interest and security in each case. The directors may fix the maximum rate which may be charged from time to time.
The supervisory committee examines the books and accounts at least quarterly, makes an annual audit and reports thereon to the annual meeting. The supervisory committee may also suspend any officer and call a meeting of the credit union to report on such suspension.
There are thus three committees in each credit union, with well-defined functions. The exceptionally low loss record of credit unions is probably partly due to this three-way system of checks, balances and administration. Another factor is that the tie of residence, association or community which must form the basis of credit union membership, seems to be conducive to a careful selection of members and results in a certain similarity of credit problems.
Another factor is that of the loyalty of a credit union member to his group. When he borrows money from his credit union he tends to remember that he is borrowing the money of his friends and neighbours. Another factor responsible for the low loss rates of credit unions is undoubtedly that all credit union legislation makes provision for at least an annual inspection of each credit union by the registrar or other government official concerned with the administration of the legislation.
Further on there is the following:
Most of the loans made by credit unions are for the purpose of meeting current expenses of the members, although as the resources increase, mortgage loans may be made.
The point on which I have taken issue with the hon. member tor Assiniboia is the fact that his whole argument is based on a 12 per cent rate of interest and as far as I can gather from the arguments he has put forward in the past three years he has established that rate only from the fact that it is the rate charged by credit unions which are on a much different basis, are much more selective, examine loans made to their members much more closely than the ordinary investor or finance company can and therefore have much more stringent control over the individual member. In fact, Mr. Speaker, even within the credit unions themselves loans, in addition to being made very carefully, generally have a provision whereby the note is endorsed by at least two members of the association. The act itself provides that

if the directors make the wrong type of loan they are in fact responsible for making the necessary repayment.
By taking an extremely unusual group such as the credit unions and adopting the 12 per cent rate of interest the hon. member has in my opinion failed to look at the realities of the situation. I feel that the result, although not intended by the hon. member, would be just the opposite. In other words, there would be a tremendous increase in loan sharks and the number of people trying to circumvent the legislation because people would not be inclined to take the great risk involved in lending money at 12 per cent.
The editorial to which I referred earlier emphasizes some of the types of individuals who borrow money from loan companies. In contrast, the credit unions scrutinize prospective members thoroughly and to a large degree seek them out for their honesty and responsibility. On the other hand, the loan association estimates that at least 20 per cent of the people who borrow from such companies require special consideration.
I referred earlier in the discussion to the fact that I was a lawyer and that in my earlier days as a young lawyer I had had occasion to follow up some of these people. The thing that amazed me was the extent of irresponsibility of the people who got that far. Although there is not too great respect, shall we say, held for lawyers when they are pursuing people on such matters, personally I took the attitude that I would try to get them to come and see me so that I could talk over the matter with them, point out that they had contracted an outstanding debt and that the best thing for them to do was to try to pay it off.
Very often there were cases where service of papers was involved. I can think of some instances where I telephoned the man concerned and said, "If you come into my office on Tuesday we can save you at least the $5 costs involved in serving the papers." I can remember an instance where the person came in on Friday. He apparently had not bothered to take the trouble to come in before and had just decided that he did not want to make the saving. I had a great deal of difficulty in understanding that attitude. I should like to clear up the impression created by the newspaper editorial. There are many good, responsible Canadian families who at times have to obtain small loans from the loan companies but I do want to accentuate the matter a bit with my own personal experience that not all people who borrow from loan companies are highly virtuous and respectable.
When I started out to practice as a lawyer I also had the experience of following up
Interest Act
members of a particular credit union. Several of them would perhaps move away, forget their problems and leave the two endorsers on the note with the responsibility of paying it. I think the hon. member for Assiniboia has not disclosed in any of his speeches on this subject during the past three years a realistic approach as to what would be a sensible rate of interest. He has merely reached out, taken a figure which he assumed would be suitable because of the specialized case of credit unions and has endeavoured to hold on to that figure very rigidly. Although he talked at great length about various iniquities, he has done nothing to support a figure of 12 per cent.
There is another factor that bothers me a great deal. Because of the risk involved to the various lending agencies, I would assume that in all likelihood the 12 per cent figure he has suggested as a maximum would tend to become the figure that prevailed. We would have a rather unfortunate situation in that regardless of the size of the loan, whether it was $300 or $3,000, the 12 per cent figure would still apply. I feel that the hon. member did not take this into consideration and that this is another indication of his relatively unrealistic attitude.
In order to clear up the difficulties as far as the editorial is concerned and the misrepresentation I felt was attributed to me, I should like to emphasize that I am in favour of having interest rates reduced but I do not feel that can be done until there is some realistic evidence to justify the establishment of a lower rate.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since I spoke on second reading of the bill an amendment has been moved which gives me the opportunity to rise again today to clear up a few misunderstandings that may have been inadvertently brought about by the hon. member. I should also like to refer to another case which I think should be placed on the record. When the hon. member read from the report of the investigating commission he mentioned the 12 per cent per annum rate of the credit unions. To clear up any misunderstanding, this is the maximum rate permitted to credit unions but in actual practice the rate charged is not nearly that high.
I think the easiest way to explain it is to take a unit of $100. If you borrow $100 from a credit union and keep it for one year you will pay $12 but if you pay it back in 12 equal instalments the interest charged will only be $6.66. Most credit unions pay an interest rebate at the end of the year according to the profit the credit union has made and there is a further reduction there. In

Interest Act
the credit union with which I was associated as treasurer tor four years the rate of rebate was 15 per cent which reduced the interest rate to $5.67 on $100. Therefore it can be seen that while the interest rate is based on a maximum of 12 per cent per annum in actual fact it does not come anywhere near that figure.
In his report he mentioned the various committees-the board of directors, the credit committee and the supervisory committee- and he mentioned that the credit committee has authority to set interest rates. That is true in one sense, but it only has authority to set interest rates from 12 per cent downward, not from 12 per cent up.
With regard to the suggestion that credit unions are a privileged group, I do not think that is actually so. But from my experience of these credit unions I know of many cases where members have been taken out of the hands of the finance company, sometimes after they have been there for many years, and after only two or three years in the credit union, with the advice and assistance given by credit union officials they have been able for the first time in many years to find their way out of the dilemma they were in. I rather resent the remark the hon. member made about the irresponsibility of some people. I think, in all fairness, it is not so much irresponsibility as a complete loss of hope. Many who have been in debt to finance companies for five, ten or fifteen years, year after year, find themselves reduced to despair.
The other matter I should like to mention today has to do not with finance companies, not with money borrowed to buy luxuries or anything of that kind, but with people buying groceries, the very basic staples of life. I have run across a case where a big chain store-not one of the national chain stores, but still a big chain store-is being very accommodating to its customers, permitting them to buy on a pay-to-pay basis and then, with the excuse that the store itself has to borrow money to pay for its stocks, charging what at first sight may be regarded as a very low interest on the loans, namely three per cent. But it should not be forgotten that there are 26 pay days in a year, and on this basis the rate of interest actually works out at no less than 72 per cent per annum.
In many cases people do not realize what is happening; they are lulled to sleep by fancy advertisements. They do not realize what they are stepping into. I became interested in this matter, so I went into it a little further. I found out that the situation is even worse than it at first appeared, because it is not even three per cent, it works out at one cent interest on the first 18 cents. So if I go

into the store today and buy groceries, and tomorrow is pay day and I pay my bill, one per cent on 18 cents works out to the astronomical figure of something like 2,000 per cent a year. This is a fantastic figure and it should be prohibited in this country. This is the purpose of this bill. Those who support it are trying to put a stop to these practices which are bleeding people white without their realizing what is happening. I think this bill should definitely go back to the committee so that we may find out how many times situations of this kind are being repeated across Canada, and put a stop to these practices once and for all.

speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for that information.
Mr. Speaker, when this matter was brought before us on June 5, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), the sponsor of the amendment to the Interest Act, spoke about "the men in grey suits". I would go a little further this afternoon, bearing in mind the tales that have been told today and in the previous debate, and call them "the men in the grey fleece suits".
What is the modus operandi of the interest shark? I would say it was an ability to play very cleverly on the nerves of potential ulcer sufferers in Canada. The snare and delusion with which he traps his victim is the promise of soothing treatment to a man or woman harassed to death by debts and anxious to consolidate them and, instead of having 25 letters a month coming to the door demanding payment, to get only one instead. And once the prey is well and truly trapped, if he falls behind in interest payments the suggestion that may be made to him is to use the same remedy all over again-to consolidate that debt, both principal and interest together, into the new loan. And so it goes on, with the 24 per cent interest snowballing downhill and dragging the unhappy sufferer along willy-nilly.

It seems to me I might perform a useful service to the people of Canada who suffer from the too rapacious demands of some loan companies to remind them that sometimes it is much better to be sued and to suffer judgment rather than sign a new note which puts them in the 24 per cent interest category, for although submission to judgment may affect credit standing, the people who go to loan companies probably have little or no credit standing anyway. As I say, it might be better for these people to accept judgment and then pay six per cent interest on that judgment rather than continue to pay 24 per cent. I throw this advice out in a modest way, to whoever may be in the hands of loan companies.
One of the useful pieces of literature associated with the subject is prepared by the superintendent of insurance for Canada who finds himself seized with the task of reporting to parliament on the activities of small loans companies and moneylenders. We have the report of this gentleman for the year ending December 31, 1956, and I believe we may expect the report for 1957 some time around the end of this year. I notice that the last report of Mr. K. R. MacGregor was dated November 1, 1957. I have examined the figures, and though I pretend to be no accountant-no expert at going through company statements-I find this fascinating reading. Take, as an example, the case of a company which enjoins Canadians never to borrow money needlessly. As of the end of 1956, the total amount of money out on loan at 24 per cent interest-this was before the last change in the Small Loans Act

was just under $50 million; in fact, it was $49,866,095. Assuming that all that money were out at any given point during the year and collecting 24 per cent interest, the total amount of interest from it would be just under $12 million. Actually, I calculated it to be $11,967,862.
Looking elsewhere in the accounts of this company as reported to parliament I find that the actual income earned on those loans was just a trifle less, namely $11,806,865. The house may be interested in the difference between those two figures. It is $160,997. In short, that figure is approximately one per cent of the total amount of interest earned by the company. It would suggest to me- although perhaps I may be wrong and may not be reading the balance sheet correctly .-that these companies are very efficient when they lend money at 24 per cent and are able to get it all back. It also suggests to me that the potential which they have to lend out is in fact lent out, because of the $160,000 figure which indicates that they are just about
Interest Act
getting the maximum use of the money for which they have potential loan customers.
Reading elsewhere from the balance sheet, I would suggest to any committee which is charged with studying this matter that the reserve for bad loans of these companies is probably too high in the light of the figures I have just given the house. However, I think the house should also know that while the major loan companies are extremely efficient in their transactions, there are smaller companies in the business of making small loans and their fate is not always a generous one. The big companies seem to take the cake in this business. For example, at page 52 of Mr. McGregor's report for the year 1956, I find that 71 companies which were in the small loans business during 1956 had a loss of $292,204 on their operations. It is true that these companies were in other fields and on those operations they made $4,637,546. But at least the figure of the loss on small loans indicates that there is some danger in this field.
My hope would be that this matter would go before the committee as recommended in the amendment of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) and I am going to support his amendment for that reason. It may be that we have even another remedy and that is to examine the English law on this matter. I do not know the constitutional implications, whether it is a jurisdiction of the federal parliament or of the provincial legislatures but I think the matter is worth looking into. As the house perhaps knows, under the English laws relating to usury I do not believe there is any particular ceiling on the amount of interest that can be charged but there is a good healthy provision that courts may be enabled to look into the whole transaction.
Yet another possible suggestion on this matter is that this and all other matters of credit policy be studied by a royal commission such as the one which was set up in Canada some 25 years ago and which led to the setting up of the Bank of Canada. As has been suggested by the premier of New Brunswick, Hon. Hugh John Flemming, such a royal commission could be charged with a good many tasks, among them the problems of Canadians in obtaining credit.
My final suggestion to the hon. member for Assiniboia and his supporters is that perhaps they might give serious consideration to amendments to the Bank Act. I am informed that at the present time the banks make no profit in the small loan business. Perhaps that is the reason why they have allowed these finance companies to spring up. They find it difficult to operate small loans departments on the 6 per cent interest that is

Interest Act
allowed. Even if they are successful in obtaining back all the money that they loaned out under small loans to customers, they still do not find it profitable for the time of the supervisors and the employees would have to be charged up against such operations.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) moved an amendment to refer this bill to the banking and commerce committee.
However, I should like to say a few words on the purpose of this bill, which is to limit to 12 per cent a year the interest charged by some finance companies.
The Interest Act, as it is drafted just now, sets no limit on the interest which can be charged in Canada. In certain fields, limitations are imposed with respect to the interest rate but they are provided for by special legislation.
An analysis of loans under the Small Loans Act, the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Bank Act, and so forth, reveals that there is no legal limit to the interest rate which finance companies may charge at the present time and anyone is free to make a loan to an individual at any rate of interest agreed by the two parties. It is also legal at the present time for a finance company to charge all costs which may be agreed upon between the purchaser of an article and the company.
No limitation is provided for in the case of the interest rate which a business undertaking can charge to finance its instalment sales. The bill now before us would set a limit with respect to the interest on all loans made for instalment buying. Like the other bill on the order paper concerning the Small Loans Act, this bill would restrict the interest rate at 12 per cent annually. If the interest rate of 24 per cent a year charged on small loans is too high, the rates of 25 per cent, 30 per cent or 40 per cent charged by some finance companies are obviously fantastic.
To have to borrow money at that rate of interest is a dreadful thing for hundreds of thousands of Canadians.
Some large commercial businesses are charging today, in Canada, for instalment purchases, a rate as high as 54 per cent a year.
The interest which government bonds yield now is in the neighbourhood of 3 per cent.
The huge sums of money now being loaned under the National Housing Act are loaned at an annual rate of interest of about 5 per cent. The rate of interest prescribed under the Farm Improvement Loans Act is 5 per

cent a year. Bank loans yield in the neighbourhood of 5 or 6 per cent per year.
If this maximum of 24 per cent charged for small loans is too high and must be lowered, an interest of 30 or even 40 per cent charged by some commercial companies is certainly exaggerated. In fact, it is four times and even eight times higher than the interest rate charged by the banks. The borrowers from those lending institutions are, in the main, the ones who can less afford such a high interest. Most of them are workers.
I am in favour of this bill to limit the interest rate of finance companies and great commercial businesses. I am supported in this by labour unions such as the CTCC which has an important branch in my constituency and whose president, at Joliette, is Mr. Marcellin Ferland.
The interest charged on loans granted to the lower income groups should be reduced to a level comparable as much as possible to the rate of interest charged borrowers who are considered to be better risks.
Say what you will of the differences that must exist between interest rates, I maintain that the disparity between an interest rate of 6 per cent asked by the banks for ordinary loans and of 24 per cent for small loans- and even 28, 30, or 40 per cent for larger loans-which is charged by some finance companies is certainly much too high.
In this country, credit unions lend money to their members at a rate of one per cent a month. In this way they can accumulate savings and pay rebates. May I also, in this house, give credit to the Caisses Populates founded in 1900 by Mr. Alphonse Desjardins, of Levis (P.Q.), and which have multiplied throughout Canada.
The slogan of these credit unions is "All for one and each for all".
There are several credit unions in my riding, and they are partly responsible for the present development of home-building.
If today a number of workers have become house-owners, it is thanks to the credit unions and the provincial law of Quebec with regard to the family home. I would strongly encourage all classes of society to go and deposit their savings in their local caisse, or union. This money helps all groups, and more especially the working class.
The number and the size of the deposits increase the confidence of the owners and the very low rates of interest attracts prospective borrowers and prevents them from falling into the nets of the lending companies.
How many workers and large families have been able to settle their housing problem thanks to credit unions?

Allow me to pay tribute to hon. Senator Cyrille Vaillancourt who has shown an exceptional devotion to the Quebec credit unions. His nobility of heart, his magnanimity and his work have allowed credit unions to spread throughout the country and to become the pride of Canada. In my constituency, in the town of Joliette, credit unions are prosperous. Their boards of directors are made up of serious and devoted men and their managers, notably Mr. Marcel Gravel and Mr. Albert Lajoie, are hard working men.
Mr. Turgeon, the manager of the Caisse Populaire de L'Assomption is a credit to his board of directors.
In Montcalm, credit unions are equally prosperous.
There are about 4,500 credit unions in our country, which lend more than $300 million to more than 1,700,000 members. The number of credit unions and the scope of their operations are ever increasing. For instance, in 1948, there were only 2,600 of them with 850,600 members. The credit union system is more flexible than that of any other finance undertaking, as far as borrowers are concerned.
They also do a fine educational and moral job by tying their financial activity with the campaign against obscene literature, for example.
There are also the rural establishment banks instituted by the clergy of Quebec and by the UCC. They make loans at a very low interest rate to sons of farmers wishing to settle on a farm and thus complete the provincial farm credit system that lends money at a record low interest rate of 2J per cent.
Credit is vital to any nation wishing to develop. Our prosperity depends upon it in large measure. A reasonable interest rate would not only permit more Canadians to satisfy their needs but would increase the purchasing power.
I hope this legislation will be adopted, as it will facilitate loans at a reasonable rate of interest. Unfortunately, low wage earners must pay high interest rates while people of means can borrow at low rates. I do not suggest that it is possible to achieve uniform rates, but I say that the discrepancy between the two is too sharp at the present time.
Loans have become more and more important in Canada through the years. A table showing the total earnings made on small loans granted by finance companies dealing with this type of business reveal that in 1941, for instance, they have earned $1,642,000. In 1946, their earnings jumped to $2,926,000, and 57071-3-110

As these hon. gentlemen to whom I have referred have pointed out, if this action were taken it would result in over 9,000 men being out of work in the coal fields, thereby constituting a serious hardship to them and their families and, in general, much economic loss to the province of Nova Scotia as a whole.
Discussions have taken place between the representatives of the company, of the labour union, of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), who is himself a member from Nova Scotia, and of course always with the concurrence of and in the presence of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois) and those discussions yesterday culminated in the meeting to which I made reference earlier today. At that meeting company officials undertook that at the end of the 25-day lay-off already announced the company would continue its normal operations providing it is compensated for the additional cost to which it would be put to maintain the excess over and above the normal stockpile.
After full consideration and on the recommendation of the minister of mines the government has decided that in order to help maintain employment the subvention policy now in existence will be extended so as to include among the cost audit items to be determined by the comptroller of the treasury the amount of the insurance stockpile and interest charges of the excess coal stockpiled this year and the government of Nova Scotia has agreed to share in these additional costs with the federal government. I am glad to report that this action will result in the company being enabled to maintain at a high level employment in the coal mines it operates.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we were very glad to hear of this move to provide continuous employment for these employees. Would the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) consider some action along the same lines in co-operation with the government of British Columbia to assist the idle coal miners in that province?

subtopic: STATEMENT ON REPORTED CUT- BACKS AND MINE CLOSURES
speechtext: I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that in this case there is a very large stockpile far in excess of the normal carryover and it was on that basis that this action was taken. In the case mentioned by the hon. gentleman I can only say that naturally consideration would have to be given on the basis of existent economic conditions within the company and the degree to which there is an excess. These would necessarily be matters to be considered in determining what course should be followed in the case of the mines to which he has made reference.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I inquire from the leader of the house what the business will be on Monday? Will he tell us what items of government business will be called on Tuesday?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday we intend to move to go into supply. There has been no agreement reached that that motion will be dealt with within one day. Should we get into supply on Monday we would take the estimates of the Department of Public Works, a few of which remain to be dealt with, and then those of the Department of Agriculture.
In the event that we do get into supply on Monday we would take on Tuesday, first, item No. 15 on today's order paper, which provides for setting up a sessional committee to deal with government-owned railways and shipping; then item No. 5, the second reading of the act to incorporate the lakehead harbour commissioners; then item No. 4, the second reading of the act to amend the Lake of the Woods Control Board Act; then item No. 12, the resolution concerning the Yukon Act, and item 11, the resolution concerning the Cape Breton Highlands national park. By the way, the departments which it is proposed to call are defence production, fisheries and mines and technical surveys.
